lessons.title: Say hello and hear Italian vowels
lessons.html:
Can-do: choose a friendly or polite greeting and introduce yourself with a familiar phrase. Prerequisites: none. New productive chunks: ciao (hi/bye with familiar people), buongiorno (good morning/day), grazie (thank you), mi chiamo … (my name is …). Recognition only: the five vowel letters. Core: orientation, sounds and first contact.

A — Orientation and a small lesson

Welcome. You can begin using Italian today. You do not need to know the alphabet first. You may listen, speak softly, or use the quiet route. Today is practice; errors help choose the next activity.

Look at two adult scenes: a friend arriving and a receptionist welcoming a visitor. “Ciao” fits the friend. “Buongiorno” is a safe polite daytime greeting for the receptionist. “Grazie” thanks someone. These phrases are not interchangeable.

Italian has five vowel letters: a, e, i, o, u. Listen to a clear model and copy one at a time. Keep a vowel steady rather than turning it into a long English letter name. The letter i has the vowel sound in the model, not the English letter name “eye”. We will learn words and sounds together.

Worked example, choosing a scene: An adult visitor meets a receptionist during the day. I choose “Buongiorno”, because it is a polite greeting. I then say “Mi chiamo Luca” — My name is Luca. “Luca” is the example person's name; use your own or an invented name.

B — Guided practice, independent practice and recap

Guided G1: Complete with buongiorno or grazie: a receptionist says hello; you answer “___”.

Guided G2: Complete with ciao or grazie: a friend passes you something; you thank them: “___”.

Independent I1: You meet a friend you know well. Choose ciao or grazie as the greeting.

Independent I2: Hide the example. Write or say a short greeting and your name to a daytime receptionist. You can pause between the two phrases.

If a speaker is available, listen to these three vowel sounds without seeing the script and point to a, i or u. This is sound recognition, not a pronunciation score. Quiet route: match printed a/i/u with the same letter on a second card; record only visual recognition.

Recap: a greeting opens the exchange; grazie expresses thanks. “Mi chiamo …” is a useful whole phrase. Do not translate it word by word yet.

Connected detail, optional: the letters e and o each represent more than one vowel quality in standard Italian. We will use word models rather than pretending five letters mean exactly five spoken vowels. This is a preview, not an exit requirement.

C — Useful phrase, mini-conversation and exit

Useful phrase: “Grazie” — Thank you.

Conversation:

  • Receptionist: Buongiorno. — Good morning/day.
  • Visitor: Buongiorno. Mi chiamo Sara. — Good morning/day. My name is Sara.
  • Receptionist: Buongiorno, Sara. — Good morning/day, Sara.
  • Visitor: Grazie. — Thank you. (The receptionist has just handed over a visitor card.)

Play visitor and replace Sara with your chosen name. Quiet route: write the visitor's two turns.

Exit E1: A different daytime receptionist greets you. Give your greeting and chosen name without looking at the dialogue.

Exit E2: Someone hands you your visitor card. Say or write the appropriate thanks.

Next action: if both meanings are clear, continue to D02 and revisit these phrases next session. If ciao/grazie are confused, use the picture contrast again with different people.

Short route: orientation, greeting example, G1, two visitor turns, E2; defer vowel comparison and E1.

lessons.title: Spell a name without memorising an alphabet
lessons.html:
Can-do: use a reference chart to spell a short name, then try a different name without a model. Prerequisite: greeting/name phrase introduced. New productive chunks: Come si scrive? (How is it written/spelled?), Si scrive … (It is written/spelled …). Letter-name use is a separate skill. Recycled: buongiorno, grazie, mi chiamo.

A — Recall and explanation

Without looking at D01, give a polite daytime greeting and say your name. Check the model afterwards. If you cannot recall it, read it once and try again with a different name; mark that attempt supported.

Letter names help when someone writes your name on a form. A letter's name is not always its sound inside a word. Italian c is called “ci”, but in casa it has a different sound. Use the chart as a tool, not a test of 21 names today.

Alphabet reference. Picture words below are recognition-only reference captions, not a required new vocabulary list. All nouns include articles. Names are given in ordinary Italian spelling; hear them before practising.

Letter Italian name Meaningful reference caption
A a l'acqua — water
B bi il bar — café/bar
C ci la casa — house/home
D di il documento — document
E e l'euro — euro
F effe la farmacia — pharmacy
G gi il gelato — ice cream
H acca l'hotel — hotel
I i l'indirizzo — address
L elle il latte — milk
M emme la mappa — map
N enne il nome — name
O o l'ora — time/hour
P pi il pane — bread
Q cu il quartiere — neighbourhood
R erre il ristorante — restaurant
S esse la stazione — station
T ti il treno — train
U u l'ufficio — office
V vu (also vi) la valigia — suitcase
Z zeta lo zaino — backpack

Also recognise J i lunga, K cappa, W doppia vu, X ics, Y ipsilon (also i greca), used in names and borrowed words. Your own name may need them. The Treccani alphabet reference gives background on the writing system; this chart is an original teaching aid.

Worked example, spelling: “Mi chiamo Mia.” A listener asks “Come si scrive?” I answer “M, I, A”: say the letter names emme, i, a. I do not read the whole word again as though it were spelling.

B — Practice and repair

G1: Use the chart to spell Lia aloud or write its letter names. G2: The names emme–i–a make which written name: Mia or Lia?

I1: Close the worked example; use the chart if needed and spell Lina. Mark chart use as support. I2: A speaker says a–elle–i. Write the name. The audio transcript stays hidden. Without a speaker, skip listening and sequence printed letter cards instead.

Recap: read a word to say it; use letter names to spell it. Reopen the chart whenever needed.

Connected detail: a doubled letter can be spelled by naming it twice; “doppia” plus the letter name is another common convention. Naming it twice is sufficient now.

C — Phrase, conversation and exit

Useful phrase: “Come si scrive?” — How is it spelled? Learn it as a chunk; its grammar comes later.

  • Visitor: Buongiorno. Mi chiamo Lina. — Good morning/day. My name is Lina.
  • Receptionist: Come si scrive? — How is it spelled?
  • Visitor: L, I, N, A. — elle, i, enne, a.
  • Receptionist: Grazie. — Thank you.

E1: With the chart closed, spell Sara using letter names. If needed, reopen the chart and mark supported rather than failing the lesson. E2: Ask someone how their name is spelled. Next action: continue to D03; review only the letters in names you actually use. Quiet route: write the letter names and two dialogue turns; spoken spelling remains unassessed.

Short route: recall, Mia example, G1, the two central dialogue turns, E2; keep the chart open.

lessons.title: A classmate and a receptionist: tu and Lei
lessons.html:
Can-do: choose an informal or polite name question and respond to it. Prerequisite: D01 name chunk; D02 chart available. New productive chunks: Come ti chiami? (What's your name? informal), Come si chiama? (What's your name? polite), piacere (pleased to meet you), arrivederci (goodbye). Dedicated speaking lesson: register and interaction. It is not a pronunciation test.

A — Recall and grammar card

Recall buongiorno and mi chiamo without the model. Use one as a greeting and the other to give your name.

Explanation: Italian can address one person with informal tu or polite Lei. For today's two questions, learn the complete phrases. “Come ti chiami?” suits a friendly classmate using tu. “Come si chiama?” suits a polite exchange at reception. A social setting can change the choice; age alone does not dictate it.

English comparison: English uses “you” in both settings; tone and wording often carry the difference. Italian also changes the grammatical form.

Urdu comparison, grammar only: Urdu distinguishes تم (tum) and آپ (aap), which can help you notice that address affects wording: “آپ کا نام کیا ہے؟” means “What is your name?” in a respectful form. The social rules and verb patterns do not map exactly onto tu and Lei. Italian polite Lei uses third-person singular verb forms; Urdu آپ has its own agreement conventions. Do not replace one form mechanically with the other.

Italian examples: “Come ti chiami?” — What's your name? (informal). “Come si chiama?” — What's your name? (polite). “Mi chiamo Nora.” — My name is Nora.

Worked example, role choice: A receptionist has begun with buongiorno and polite address. To ask their name, choose “Come si chiama?” The solved example uses a receptionist; practise the new role below.

B — Guided and independent interaction

G1: A friendly adult classmate has suggested using tu. Complete: Come ___ chiami? (ti/si). G2: At a service desk using polite address, choose Come ti chiami? / Come si chiama?

I1: An unfamiliar adult teacher begins a polite introduction. Say an appropriate greeting and ask their name. I2: A classmate says “Ciao, mi chiamo Eva. E tu?” The supplied “E tu?” means “And you?” Give your own name and say pleased to meet you.

Listen/replay if possible. Check: did you ask a name question, answer the partner, and keep the chosen register? Do not judge an accent from the transcript.

Recap: choose a complete question for the relationship and keep it consistent. A grammatical mismatch is not a personal failing; repair the phrase and try again.

Connected detail: polite Lei can address a man or a woman. The capital L is a writing convention used to signal politeness, not a different spoken sound; lowercase lei is also found. Full verb and pronoun patterns come later.

C — Two scripts and a fresh role-play

Useful phrase: “Piacere.” — Pleased to meet you.

Informal script:

  • Nora: Ciao! Mi chiamo Nora. Come ti chiami? — Hi! My name is Nora. What's your name?
  • Ali: Mi chiamo Ali. Piacere. — My name is Ali. Pleased to meet you.
  • Nora: Piacere. — Pleased to meet you.
  • Ali: Ciao! — Bye!

Polite script:

  • Visitor: Buongiorno. Mi chiamo Ali. — Good morning/day. My name is Ali.
  • Staff member: Buongiorno. Mi chiamo Anna. — Good morning/day. My name is Anna.
  • Visitor: Piacere. — Pleased to meet you.
  • Staff member: Piacere. Arrivederci. — Pleased to meet you. Goodbye.

E1: New role: at an adult-course registration desk, greet staff, give your chosen name and ask theirs using polite address. No model open. E2: New role: a course partner is using tu. Ask their name, then respond “pleased to meet you” after they answer. If practising alone, leave a pause for the imagined partner. Quiet route: write each role's turns; mark S/P unassessed.

Next action: if ti/si is mixed, use a two-column role card and a new person's name next visit. Continue other successful work. Short route: recall, grammar examples, G1, informal three-turn exchange, E2.

lessons.title: Predict useful sounds: c/ch and g/gh
lessons.html:
Can-do: sort common c/g patterns and use a polite repetition request. Prerequisites: vowel awareness; greetings. New productive items: il caffè (coffee), il gelato (ice cream), Può ripetere? (Could you repeat?). Recycled/receptive: la casa from alphabet chart. Contrast-only: la chiave (key), gli spaghetti (spaghetti), il giro (turn/tour). These contrast words are not required for free recall today.

A — Recall and explanation

Recall a polite greeting and the polite name question. Listen to a model of ciao and caffè if available. They begin with the same letter but different sounds.

For the common patterns practised today: c before a/o/u has /k/; c before e/i has /tʃ/, approximately the first sound in English “chair”. ch before e/i keeps /k/. g before a/o/u has /g/; g before e/i has /dʒ/, approximately English “job”; gh before e/i keeps /g/. Listen to whole-word models rather than making English spellings your pronunciation target. These basic patterns are supported by Treccani on c and g.

Worked example, sorting: “la casa” goes into /k/: c is followed by a. “il gelato” goes into /dʒ/: g is followed by e. Say them only after hearing a model if you are unsure.

B — Practice and repair

G1: Choose /k/ or /tʃ/ for the c at the beginning of il caffè. G2: Choose /g/ or /dʒ/ for gh in gli spaghetti. Focus on gh only; the article gli is a later sound lesson.

I1: Sort la chiave and il giro: which has /k/, which /dʒ/? I2: A speaker reads one word from each pair; choose the written word: caffè/gelato, then casa/chiave. Do not infer sound from a visible transcript. Quiet route: identify the spelling pattern on the page instead; listening remains unassessed.

Recap: h in ch/gh changes how you interpret the preceding letter before e/i; it does not add an English h sound in these patterns.

Connected detail: in ciao, i helps signal the consonant sound and is not a separate full “ee” syllable. Not every written i behaves identically. Later sound lessons will cover sc, gn and gli separately; today's rule is not a complete Italian pronunciation system. See Treccani on digraphs.

C — Phrase, café script and exit

Useful phrase: “Può ripetere?” — Could you repeat? A fixed polite request; its modal grammar comes later.

  • Staff: Caffè? — Coffee?
  • Visitor: Può ripetere? — Could you repeat?
  • Staff: Caffè? — Coffee?
  • Visitor: Caffè, grazie. — Coffee, thank you.

E1: New printed contrast-only words with meanings supplied: il cane (dog), la cena (dinner). Sort their initial c into /k/ or /tʃ/ without the model. You are not being asked to recall their meanings. E2: Respond when you have not understood a staff member's question by requesting repetition politely.

Next action: if the pattern is clear but listening uncertain, keep reading evidence and schedule audio discrimination repair. Short route: recall, c/ch explanation, G1, café script, E2; defer g/gh to another session if necessary.

lessons.title: Hear the beat: stress and double consonants
lessons.html:
Can-do: notice the stressed syllable in familiar words and discriminate a practised single/double contrast. Prerequisite: vowels; D04 sound models. Productive: per favore (please); il pane (bread). Recognition-only contrast: la pala (shovel), la palla (ball); la penna (pen) is a meaningful double-consonant example, not another productive requirement today.

A — Recall and explanation

Recall the meaning of il caffè, then say or read Può ripetere? Hear a speaker model CA-sa. The prominent syllable is the stressed one. In caffè, stress falls on the last syllable: caf-FÈ. The accent is part of the correct spelling.

Double consonants can change a word. In pala/palla, both stress the first syllable, but the l in palla is held longer. Do not add an extra vowel between the consonants. This is a listening and articulation distinction, not a rule to shout a syllable or make the whole word twice as long. Treccani on double letters provides background.

Worked example, marking stress: hear “la casa”. Write CA-sa on your practice line. Normal spelling remains la casa. For la palla, hear the longer l and match it to the ball picture. The model illustrates the task before the new listening order.

B — Practice and repair

G1: Hear il caffè; choose CAF-fè / caf-FÈ. G2: Look at the ball picture and choose la pala / la palla, then hear the correct word.

I1: Hear la pala / la palla in a hidden four-item sequence and choose shovel or ball for each. I2: Hear la penna and il pane; mark PEN-na or pen-NA, then PA-ne or pa-NE. Definitions are supplied, so this tests sound attention rather than unfamiliar meaning.

If you can record, imitate palla after the model, replay it, and compare consonant duration. Self-comparison is practice, not a validated rating. Quiet route: identify the written double consonant and written accent; record spelling observation only.

Recap: stress is the prominent syllable; a double consonant is a sound-length distinction. Neither is assessed by a successful transcription alone.

Connected detail: stress often occurs on the penultimate syllable, but there are many exceptions. Learn stress with each word. An accent marks final stress in caffè; most internal stress is not written.

C — Phrase, conversation and exit

Useful phrase: “Per favore.” — Please.

  • Customer: Caffè, per favore. — Coffee, please.
  • Staff: Caffè? — Coffee?
  • Customer: Caffè, grazie. — Coffee, thank you.
  • Staff: Prego. — You're welcome. (Prego is recognition-only today.)

E1: Hear two new-order items from the taught pala/palla pair. Choose the picture for each. This is fresh order, not proof of generalisation to every double consonant. E2: Without the line open, give a brief polite coffee request including please. If audio is not available, use E2 and leave E1 unassessed.

Next action: incorrect E1 → practise one contrast again with model/replay next visit; avoid adding more pairs. Short route: recall, double-consonant explanation, G2, request exchange, E2; save stress work for the next visit.

lessons.title: Learn a noun with its article: il and la
lessons.html:
Can-do: use article+noun pairs for four familiar things. Prerequisites: recognition of casa, caffè, pane; la pasta introduced below. New productive item: la pasta (pasta). Consolidate il caffè, la casa, il pane as whole pairs. Dedicated grammar lesson: a small subset of definite articles, not the complete system.

A — Recall and complete grammar card

Look at a coffee cup and a home picture. Recall their Italian words if you can; then reveal il caffè and la casa. If the article is new to your recall, that is today's learning target.

Simple explanation: Italian nouns have grammatical gender. A definite article often corresponds to English “the”. Today learn il caffè, il pane, la casa and la pasta as pairs. Il is masculine singular and la is feminine singular for the examples chosen. We will learn other article forms later. A noun's grammatical gender is not a judgement about the object or a person's identity.

English comparison: English “the” does not change for coffee versus house. Italian articles can change with gender, number and the following sounds.

Urdu comparison: Urdu also has grammatical gender: “یہ گھر بڑا ہے” — This house is big; “یہ کتاب بڑی ہے” — This book is big. بڑا / بڑی show agreement. Urdu has no directly equivalent mandatory definite article matching Italian il/la. Italian la casa is feminine, while Urdu گھر is masculine: never copy a noun's gender from Urdu into Italian.

Italian examples with meanings: “il pane” — the bread; “la pasta” — the pasta; “la casa” — the house; “il caffè” — the coffee.

Worked example, article choice: Picture: a coffee cup. I choose il + caffè → il caffè, because caffè belongs to the masculine pair learned today. The final letter alone does not give me a safe universal gender rule.

B — Grammar practice, independent use and recap

G1: Choose il/la for casa using the pair card if needed. G2: Complete ___ pane using the pair card if needed.

I1: Hide the cards. Write ___ pasta and ___ casa. I2: Match two printed labels, il pane and il caffè, to bread and coffee pictures; then say or write both complete labels without the choices visible.

Recap: retain the article with the noun. If you wrote il casa, replace the pair with la casa and retrieve it once with a different house picture. Do not learn “all -a words are feminine” as an absolute rule.

Connected detail: il/la are only part of the system. Later you will meet lo and l', then plurals such as i and le. They are previews here and not required in the exit.

C — Phrase, conversation and exit

Useful phrase: “Il caffè, per favore.” — The coffee, please, when choosing a visible coffee. For ordering a new coffee, the natural “Un caffè, per favore” comes in M2. Make the pictured selection context clear.

  • Staff: Il pane o la pasta? — The bread or the pasta? (o = or, supplied.)
  • Customer: La pasta, per favore. — The pasta, please.
  • Staff: La pasta. — The pasta.
  • Customer: Grazie. — Thank you.

E1: New picture: a different loaf. Write its complete Italian label without a word bank. E2: New picture: a different plate of pasta. Give its complete label. Quiet route: write both. Optional listening: identify which item a partner offers without reading the script; do not count this unless heard.

Next action: if article pairing fails, put the complete pair in the journal and practise with a new picture next visit. If only spelling fails, retain recognition success. Short route: recall, grammar card examples, G1, two selection turns, E1. Read the comparison on the next visit if time is short.

lessons.title: Write a first message and use feedback
lessons.html:
Can-do: write a short greeting and introduction, then repair one real error and transfer the change. Prerequisites: D01/D03 name and greeting chunks; basic letter access. New productive chunk: Sono di … (I am from …), taught before use. Dedicated writing lesson: two or three brief sentences, not an essay. D06 articles are reviewed separately so a name message is not overloaded with unrelated nouns.

A — Recall, small lesson and worked message

Recall the two article+noun labels il pane and la casa using different pictures. Reveal them after attempting. Then recall mi chiamo without a word bank.

Today write to an adult Italian-course group. Include a greeting, your name and optionally your city of origin. You may invent both name and city. “Sono di Lahore” means “I am from Lahore.” This is a useful chunk today; full essere forms come in M1. Use capitals for a sentence start, a person's name and a city name. End a sentence with a full stop.

Worked example, different writer: “Ciao! Mi chiamo Nora. Sono di Bari.” — Hi! My name is Nora. I am from Bari. It includes a greeting, a name and an origin. We will not copy Nora's facts in the independent task.

Grammar card, a small connected point: Italian often allows a subject pronoun to be omitted because the verb form and context help show who is speaking. English normally needs “I” in “I am”. Urdu “میں لاہور سے ہوں” (I am from Lahore) includes میں (main); omission can occur in context, but the patterns are not identical. Compare Italian “Io sono di Bari” and “Sono di Bari”: both mean “I am from Bari”; io can add emphasis. Do not delete pronouns mechanically or treat every omission as correct. Quick practice: is “Io sono di Bari” wrong merely because io is written? Answer: no. Pronoun omission is optional detail here, not a requirement in the exit.

B — Guided draft, independent draft and complete feedback example

G1: Complete: Ciao! Mi ___ Amal. (chiamo/chiama). G2: Put these supplied words in order: di / Sono / Roma. The model demonstrated the sentence type with Bari; this uses a different city.

I1, original attempt: hide the example. Write 2–3 short sentences to your new course group: greet them, give a chosen name, and say where you are from if you can. There is no minimum word count. I2, self-check: underline your name chunk and check capitals and sentence endings. Save the original before changing it.

Worked feedback, separate fictional learner:

  • Original: “ciao mi chiama Amir. Sono di Lahore.”
  • Minimal correction: “Ciao! Mi chiamo Amir. Sono di Lahore.”
  • Natural A1 alternative: “Ciao! Sono Amir. Sono di Lahore.”
  • Actual errors: begin Ciao with a capital and separate the greeting; mi chiamo is the first-person name chunk, while mi chiama does not express the intended introduction here.
  • Optional style: Sono Amir is an alternative introduction, not a required improvement. The origin remains Lahore. No identity or factual changes are made.
  • Targeted repair: complete “Mi ___ Hana” using chiamo/chiama. Then write one introduction for the fictional person Hana without the choices.
  • Fresh attempt: a different course partner asks for a written introduction for their study group. Write a new greeting plus your chosen name; do not copy the Amir correction. Add origin only if you want to.

Apply this same feedback sequence to I1. If no coach/reviewer is available, use the self-check and model with the label self-reviewed; do not claim an independent automatic assessment. Preserve correct wording and accept valid alternatives. When meaning is unclear, ask rather than inventing it.

Recap: a clear two-sentence message is useful. Repair the important error before adding more language.

Connected detail: the optional pronoun card above shows that “Io sono …” and “Sono …” can both be correct. Do not flag one as an error solely because the other is shorter.

C — Phrase, conversation and fresh exit

Useful phrase: “Sono di …” — I am from …

  • Teacher: Buongiorno. Come si chiama? — Good morning/day. What's your name?
  • Learner: Mi chiamo Amal. — My name is Amal.
  • Teacher: Piacere. — Pleased to meet you.
  • Learner: Piacere. Sono di Lahore. — Pleased to meet you. I am from Lahore.

The teacher models polite address; the name response itself works with tu and Lei. Quiet route: write the learner turns. Speaking evidence needs an actual spoken attempt.

E1: For a different audience, an adult course receptionist, write a polite greeting and chosen name with the model closed. You may include an origin. E2: After feedback, introduce a different fictional person using that person's own voice, with a different name. Do not use third-person description; imagine you are that person. If tired, save E2 for the next visit and record the delay.

lessons.title: Questions & non: change the message
lessons.goal: Ask a basic question and place non before a simple finite verb.
lessons.intro: Questions help you confirm a name, find a place and repair a misunderstanding. Learn complete question phrases and then notice their parts. In writing, a question mark helps; actual question intonation needs heard examples later.
rules: Simple yes/no questions
Lei è Amal? Hai un libro? Italian does not add English do/does in these examples. Context and spoken intonation help identify a question.
Simple negation
Put non before the finite verb: Non sono Amal. Non ho un libro. In Non lo so, a pronoun intervenes; “immediately before the verb with no exceptions” would be too strong.
Useful question words
Chi? = who; dove? = where; quando? = when; come? = how; perché? = why/because; quanto? = how much/how many in its appropriate forms.
Useful complete chunks
Dove abiti? = Where do you live, informally? Come si chiama? = What is your name, politely? Do not substitute a different question word without checking the whole construction.

lessons.title: Numbers: price, time or a code?
lessons.goal: Choose how to read a number from its purpose, preserving zeros in codes.
lessons.intro: The same digits can do different jobs. A price is an amount of money; a phone number identifies a line; a clock shows a time. Identify the context before choosing Italian words. The prices below are invented teaching examples.
rules: Amounts and spelling
Uno, due, tre; ventuno, ventotto; ventitré has a written accent. Before a masculine noun use un libro; with euro, un euro. Tre euros is tre euro: euro stays unchanged.
Price format
€2,50 → due euro e cinquanta centesimi. A decimal comma is common in Italian. Do not read the cents as a phone code.
Clock agreement
È l’una; sono le due; sono le quattordici. Alle due means at two. A clear 24-hour clock avoids ambiguity about morning/afternoon.
Codes, phones and dates

Read the practice code 004 as zero zero quattro. For telephone spelling, digit by digit is a clear beginner strategy; native grouping varies. Italian numeric dates normally use day/month/year: 03/04 is 3 April.
lessons.english: English often writes a decimal point in 2.50; Italian commonly uses 2,50. English number/date conventions depend on region, so confirm an ambiguous date instead of assuming.
lessons.urdu: دو کتابیں corresponds in meaning to due libri; noun patterns differ. دو بجے means at two o’clock. A money amount, a time and a code also have distinct purposes in Urdu; their word forms do not determine Italian clock agreement.

bridge.note: Italian uses plural sono for le due, while English uses it is. This Urdu time expression groups words differently; the boxes show a comparison, not interchangeable parts.

lessons.title: Prepositions: a Roma, in Italia, al bar
lessons.goal: Learn useful place phrases and combine a preposition with an article.
lessons.intro: A preposition connects a place, person or purpose to the sentence. Store a short phrase rather than a single English translation: a Roma, in Italia, al bar. A place can have different constructions in different contexts.
rules: Common destination/location phrases
Vado a Roma; sono a Roma. Vado in Italia; sono in Italia. These city/country patterns are useful starters, not a complete atlas of place constructions.
Purpose and origin
Un biglietto per Bari = a ticket to Bari; sono di Bari = I am from Bari. Learn the governing expression, not “to always equals a”.
Combine a and articles
a + il = al; a + lo = allo; a + la = alla; a + l’ = all’; a + i = ai; a + gli = agli; a + le = alle.
Other common combinations
di + il = del; da + il = dal; in + il = nel; su + il = sul. Col/con il can occur; do not force every preposition into an identical contraction pattern.
lessons.english: English at/to/in does not uniquely select Italian a/in/da. “At the café” is al bar, while “in Italy” is in Italia. Learn the noun phrase and situation together.
lessons.urdu: Urdu commonly puts a postposition after the noun: روم میں, دفتر میں. Italian puts a/in before the place. “میں” can be the pronoun I or the postposition in, depending on context; their identical spelling does not make them the same role.

bridge.note: The first Urdu میں is I; the second is part of the place phrase. Treat دفتر میں as a unit and compare it with in ufficio.

lessons.title: Possessives & c’è / ci sono
lessons.goal: Describe what belongs to someone and what exists in a room.
lessons.intro: La sua casa can mean his house or her house. Sua agrees with casa, not with the owner. To say what is in the house, use c’è for one thing and ci sono for more than one. These are related room-description tools with different jobs.
rules: Agree with the possessed noun
Il mio libro / la mia penna / i miei libri / le mie penne. The noun controls the possessive form.
Owner and context
La sua penna can mean his/her pen, or your pen in polite address. Context resolves the owner; sua alone does not identify an owner’s gender.
Family pattern has limits

Common singular unmodified family nouns often omit the article with a possessive: mio fratello, mia sorella. Plurals normally include it: i miei fratelli. Do not extend omission to every modified form or loro.
There is / there are
C’è una sedia; ci sono due sedie. C’è is ci + è. C’è una penna describes existence; è una penna identifies something.
lessons.english: English his/her marks the owner; Italian suo/sua agrees with the owned noun. English there is/are gives a useful meaning comparison for c’è/ci sono, but ci has other functions later.
lessons.urdu: اس کا گھر / اس کی کتاب illustrates agreement linked to the possessed expression in these examples. Italian adds its own articles and family exceptions. کمرے میں ایک کرسی ہے corresponds to there is a chair in the room; word order differs.

bridge.note: Italian casa is feminine, Urdu گھر masculine. The form follows each language’s noun, not an assumed shared gender or the owner’s gender.

lessons.title: Word families: -mente, -zione & -ità
lessons.goal: Use English word-family clues safely, checking meaning and spelling.
lessons.intro: A familiar-looking ending can help you notice a word. It cannot generate a reliable translation for every English word. A family word such as famiglia is not made by adding an Italian-looking ending to English family.
rules: Adjective to manner adverb
Many adverbs use -mente: lento → lenta → lentamente; rapido → rapida → rapidamente. The adverb normally does not agree: parla lentamente; parlano lentamente.
Some -e adjectives
Facile → facilmente; normale → normalmente. Adjectives ending in -le or -re after a vowel often lose final e before -mente. Learn exceptions and usage, not a blind spelling machine.
Cognate clues

Information → informazione; education → educazione is a warning because Italian educazione often means upbringing/manners; university → università and quality → qualità show -ity/-ità clues. Stressed -ità nouns keep the same written form in the plural: le università.

English -ly is not always an adverb (friendly is an adjective). Italian bene and male do not need -mente. Family = famiglia; familiare/familiari belongs to its related family, with context-specific senses. Do not invent familioso from English family.
lessons.english: Ask what job the English word does before using a suffix clue. “A slow train” needs an adjective; “speak slowly” needs an adverb. Similar spelling can hide a different meaning: a cognate is a lead to check, not an automatic translation.
lessons.urdu: آہستہ بولیں conveys speak slowly, but آہستہ does not teach the Italian suffix -mente. خاندان / گھرانہ can express family in different contexts; their morphology does not generate famiglia or familiare. Use the comparison to notice meaning, not to manufacture endings.

lessons.title: Alphabet, vowels & the syllable model
lessons.goal: Separate letter names from word sounds, then build a word in syllables.
lessons.intro: Italian has 21 core alphabet letters. J, K, W, X and Y also appear in names and borrowed words. You can use greetings immediately; learning the alphabet is a reference skill, not a gate that must be passed before speaking.

A a; B bi; C ci; D di; E e; F effe; G gi; H acca; I i; L elle; M emme; N enne; O o; P pi; Q cu; R erre; S esse; T ti; U u; V vu (also vi); Z zeta. Extras: J i lunga, K cappa, W doppia vu, X ics, Y ipsilon (also i greca).

Our syllable model

1. Look at the normal word. 2. Break it into the supplied syllable boxes. 3. Notice the stressed box. 4. Rejoin smoothly. Example: amica → a–MI–ca → amica. Capitals in a model mark stress, not normal spelling.
Keep the last vowel
Pane ends with e; amico ends with o. H is silent in ho/ha and has spelling functions in ch/gh. A letter name and its sound in a word can differ.

Italian i is the vowel represented by /i/, with a heard Italian model.

lessons.goal: Use checked syllable divisions instead of cutting a word after every letter.
lessons.intro: A syllable has a vowel centre, but counting vowel letters is not enough. Some vowel sequences belong to one syllable; others form two. Our boxes use conventional written syllable divisions as a learning scaffold. They are not a narrow phonetic transcription or a complete account of spoken boundaries.
rules: A single consonant often starts the next syllable
Ca-sa, pa-ne, a-mi-ca. Build around the vowel centres, rather than reading isolated consonants.
Written doubles divide
Pal-la, pen-na, caf-fè. Keep the consonant long across the boundary; do not add a pause or an extra vowel. Cq also separates in conventional spelling division, as in ac-qua.
Some groups stay together
Li-bro and scuo-la. Written ch, gh and palatal gn/gl/sc groups stay together in conventional division. Do not split chiave into c-hi-a-ve.
Diphthong versus hiatus
Chia-ve and I-ta-lia have vowel sequences inside a single syllable in these examples. Pa-u-ra and po-e-ta keep two vowel centres separate. Stress and the particular word matter: use a checked model.

lessons.title: Punctuation: sentences, commas & quotations
lessons.goal: Use sentence marks and simple commas without breaking the sentence’s grammar.
lessons.intro: Punctuation organises meaning. It is not only a record of where you happen to breathe. The exercises ask for specific small edits, because longer messages can have several valid punctuation choices. Exact-edit tasks preserve punctuation when checking answers.
rules: Full stops and questions
A statement can end with a full stop: Sono qui. A direct question uses ?: Lei è qui? Use ! selectively for an exclamation. Put a space after normal sentence punctuation, not before it.
Lists and direct address
Ho pane, pasta e acqua. Sara, vieni qui! Commas separate these list items and set off a person being addressed. Do not insert one between subject and verb: Sara studia.
Colons and quotation marks

A colon can introduce direct speech: Sara dice: «Ciao!» Italian quotation styles can use «…» or “…” depending on house style. Keep opening/closing marks paired; this course supplies the exact style for each exercise.
Useful extensions

A semicolon can link closely connected clauses or organise a complex list. Parentheses enclose an aside; an ellipsis consists of three dots. These are optional extensions, not an instruction to fill a short A1 message with punctuation.

Caffè, università and perché keep their final accents. È is the verb is; e means and. Sì means yes; si has other grammatical uses. Standard spellings here use è/caffè with grave è and perché with acute é.
Apostrophes

Un’amica, l’amico and c’è show elision. Un amico has no apostrophe. Un po’ is the conventional shortening of poco: write the apostrophe, not pò. Standard edited Italian uses qual è without an apostrophe.
Capitals

Capitalise sentence beginnings and personal/place names: Ciao, Sara. Sono a Roma. Italian normally writes language names, weekdays and months lowercase: italiano, lunedì, ottobre. Contexts such as headings and names can differ.
Self-check without changing facts
Keep the writer’s chosen name/city. Correct the specific spelling or punctuation error; do not replace the whole message because another style sounds smoother. Accents are not decorations.

lessons.html:
Goal

Distinguish stress accents, apostrophes and capitalisation in short messages.

A written accent and an apostrophe do different jobs. An accent can mark stress or distinguish words; an apostrophe can mark an omitted vowel or a conventional shortening. Normal spelling stays separate from our capitalised syllable models.

Rules and useful limits

Written accents

Caffè, università and perché keep their final accents. È is the verb is; e means and. Sì means yes; si has other grammatical uses. Standard spellings here use è/caffè with grave è and perché with acute é.

Apostrophes

Un’amica, l’amico and c’è show elision. Un amico has no apostrophe. Un po’ is the conventional shortening of poco: write the apostrophe, not pò. Standard edited Italian uses qual è without an apostrophe.

Capitals

Capitalise sentence beginnings and personal/place names: Ciao, Sara. Sono a Roma. Italian normally writes language names, weekdays and months lowercase: italiano, lunedì, ottobre. Contexts such as headings and names can differ.

Self-check without changing facts

Keep the writer’s chosen name/city. Correct the specific spelling or punctuation error; do not replace the whole message because another style sounds smoother. Accents are not decorations.

Worked example

Original: “ciao sono di roma.” Minimal spelling repair: “Ciao, sono di Roma.” The comma suits this greeting structure; “Ciao! Sono di Roma.” is also a valid reformulation. For an exact-edit exercise, follow the named edit instead of rewriting freely.

Common mistakes

  • un pò → un po’ uses an apostrophe, not a grave accent.
  • qual’è → qual è is the standard edited form taught here.

Grammar comparison

English capitalises I and Italian as a language name. Italian writes io and italiano lowercase except at the start of a sentence or in another capitalising context. Urdu script has no uppercase/lowercase distinction; that does not remove Italian capitalisation rules. Urdu punctuation conventions are not a mechanical template for Italian marks.

Practice route

Use the syllable model: normal word → split → notice stress → rejoin. For writing lessons, make the named small edit, then review a fresh sentence. Choose Try it for the six saved exercises. A correct printed answer does not establish correct articulation. Record/replay is optional self-practice; no listening or pronunciation rating is assigned. A shorter visit can cover the worked example and guided item only.
lessons.alt: Sound–spelling reference chart

grammar.title: Tu, polite Lei and plural voi
grammar.html: Italian chooses forms for relationship and number: tu is informal singular; Lei is polite singular and takes third-person singular; voi addresses several people. English uses you in more than one role. Urdu تم and آپ can help notice address, but social conventions and agreement do not map one-to-one. Italian polite Lei can address any gender. “Come ti chiami?” — What's your name? informal; “Come si chiama?” — polite; “Come vi chiamate?” — plural. Check: receptionist using polite address, Lei ___ Amal? → è. Fresh: friendly classmate Tu ___ Amal? → sei. Don't treat capitalisation alone as proof of intended meaning in speech.

grammar.title: Essere: identity, description and location
grammar.html: Forms: sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono. “Sono Amal” — I am Amal; “Lei è qui” — She is here / You are here politely; “Siamo a casa” — We are at home. English be also changes, but its forms do not correspond letter by letter. Urdu “میں یہاں ہوں” and “وہ یہاں ہے” express I am here / he-she is here; Urdu distinctions are not the Italian person table. Use context for sono, which can be I am or they are. Check: Noi ___ qui → siamo; loro ___ qui → sono. Fresh: Tu ___ a casa → sei. Not all English be expressions use essere: ho fame.

grammar.title: Avere: possession and fixed expressions
grammar.html: Forms: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno. “Ho un libro” — I have a book; “Ho fame” — I am hungry; “Ha vent'anni” — He/she is twenty. English be in hunger/age is not a reason to choose essere. Urdu possession “میرے پاس کتاب ہے” and hunger “مجھے بھوک لگی ہے” use their own constructions, not an Italian verb-selection rule. Pair meaning with person: io ho versus Lei ha. Check: Lei ___ una domanda → ha; io ___ freddo → ho. Fresh: Voi ___ un libro → avete. Sono stanco/stanca uses essere: do not extend “all feelings take avere”. H is silent but required in these forms.

grammar.title: Articles, gender, number and agreement
grammar.html: Learn la casa/le case, il libro/i libri, lo studente/gli studenti, l'amica/le amiche. Articles depend on gender/number and initial sounds. Adjective examples: camera piccola, libri piccoli. English the does not make these distinctions. Urdu also has gender/agreement, e.g. “بڑا گھر” and “بڑی کتاب”, but gender may differ: Italian casa feminine, Urdu گھر masculine. There is no matching mandatory Urdu definite article. Check: la camera piccolo/piccola → piccola. Fresh: two small houses → due case piccole. Indefinite un amico has no apostrophe; un'amica derives from una before a vowel. Common endings are tendencies, not exception-free gender rules.

grammar.title: Numbers, dates, prices and codes
grammar.html: Quantity: ventitré libri; price €2,50: due euro e cinquanta centesimi; code 020: zero due zero; clock 14:00: le quattordici. English conventions vary by region; don't import US date order into Italian 03/04, normally 3 April. Urdu number words and noun forms do not determine Italian forms: “دو کتابیں” corresponds in meaning to due libri, not identical structure. “È l'una” versus “Sono le due” marks clock agreement. Check: read 004 as a code → zero zero quattro. Fresh price €1,00 → un euro. Codes retain leading zeros; price shorthand is context-bound. See the number clinic for practice.

grammar.title: Possessives and there is/are
grammar.html: “La mia casa” — my house; “mio fratello” — my brother, common singular unmodified family pattern. Learn possessive agreement with the thing possessed, not the owner's gender: la sua casa can mean his or her house. English his/her marks owner differently. Urdu “اس کا گھر” / “اس کی کتاب” also shows agreement with the possessed expression in these examples, but article/family conventions differ. C'è una sedia / ci sono due sedie = there is/are. Check: two books → ci sono due libri. Fresh: his/her room → la sua camera. Do not turn family article omission into a rule for plurals or every modified family noun.

grammar.title: Present conjugation
grammar.html: Parlare: parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano. Prendere: prendo/prendi/prende/prendiamo/prendete/prendono. Dormire and capire illustrate different -ire families: dormo versus capisco. English usually has fewer present person changes. Urdu “میں بولتا ہوں” / “میں بولتی ہوں” distinguishes speaker gender here; Italian parlo does not. “Parlo italiano” — I speak Italian. Irregular essere/avere need their own forms. Check: noi + parlare → parliamo; io + capire → capisco. Fresh: loro + dormire → dormono. Identify person and verb family before using an ending; do not apply -isc to every -ire verb.

grammar.title: Reflexives and routine
grammar.html: “Mi alzo alle sette” — I get up at seven; “Si alza alle otto” — He/she gets up at eight; “Ci alziamo” — We get up. Reflexive pronouns and verb person work together. English often uses a simple verb where Italian uses a pronominal one. Urdu “میں اٹھتا ہوں” / “میں اٹھتی ہوں” also does not supply an equivalent Italian mi in a word-for-word way. Learn a whole routine phrase, not “mi means my”. Check: io mi alzo → noi ci alziamo. Fresh: tu ti alzi. Reciprocity is a related but distinct use: ci incontriamo means we meet each other. Some pronominal verbs are not literally self-directed actions.

grammar.title: Prepositions and basic instructions
grammar.html: “Vado a Roma”, “Vado in Italia”, “Un biglietto per Bari”, “Sono dal medico.” Italian prepositions depend on a phrase and context; English to/in/at cannot be substituted mechanically. Urdu often uses postpositions, e.g. “روم میں” (in Rome), unlike Italian a/in before the noun. “Vai dritto” informal; “Vada dritto” polite. Check: Vado ___ Roma → a; un biglietto ___ Bari → per. Fresh: Sono ___ Italia → in. Later combine articles: di+il=del, a+il=al, in+il=nel, su+il=sul; learn full families in context. Avoid a claim that one destination preposition covers every place.

grammar.title: Modal plus infinitive
grammar.html: “Posso parlare?” — May/can I speak? “Devo studiare” — I must study; “Voglio capire” — I want to understand. Change the modal for person; keep the following verb infinitive in this pattern. English also has modal constructions but adds to with want, not can. Urdu “میں پڑھ سکتا ہوں” or “مجھے پڑھنا ہے” expresses related meanings with different structures; no one ending maps to all Italian modals. Check: devo studio/studiare → studiare. Fresh polite request: Lei può venire? — Can you come? Don't present potere/dovere/volere as identical in meaning or full usage. Vorrei is a polite fixed request first, conditional later.

grammar.title: Passato prossimo and auxiliary choice
grammar.html: Ho comprato / sono arrivata describe completed events in familiar contexts. Avere + participle is common with direct objects; many intransitives use essere, others avere. Learn verb+auxiliary together. With essere, participles agree: arrivato/arrivata/arrivati/arrivate. English have in present perfect is not a universal translation guide. Urdu “میں آیا” / “میں آئی” shows gender in these examples, but Urdu tense/aspect and auxiliary patterns are not Italian's. Check: Sara è arrivato/arrivata → arrivata; ho comprato. Fresh noi + visitare → abbiamo visitato. “All movement uses essere” fails for ho camminato. More advanced object-pronoun agreement needs separate instruction.

grammar.title: Imperfetto and narrative viewpoint
grammar.html: “Studiavo quando Sara è arrivata.” Imperfetto gives background/ongoing or repeated situations; passato prossimo presents bounded events in this narrative. English past progressive/used to can help but do not cover every use. Urdu “میں پڑھ رہا تھا” / “میں پڑھ رہی تھی” illustrates ongoing past; copying its auxiliaries does not produce Italian morphology. “Da bambino andavo a scuola a piedi” — As a child I used to walk to school. Check: ongoing waiting + call → Aspettavo quando ha telefonato. Fresh repeated past routine → Ogni giorno studiavo. Duration alone does not determine the tense. Advanced prose can shift viewpoint and use other past tenses.

grammar.title: Future and arrangements
grammar.html: Parlerò, prenderò, dormirò; common irregular sarò, avrò, andrò. “Domani lavoro” can also describe an arrangement; “Domani lavorerò” selects a future presentation. English will, going to and present arrangements do not map uniquely. Urdu “میں کل کام کروں گا” / “کروں گی” marks future with gender/person features differing from Italian lavorerò. Check: io + avere future → avrò. Fresh noi + parlare → parleremo. Future can also express conjecture in context: Sarà a casa may mean “He/she is probably at home”, not simply a later location. Introduce this after basic plans; don't assume every future form has a time prediction meaning.

grammar.title: Object pronouns and comparisons
grammar.html: Lo/la/li/le can replace direct objects: il libro → lo leggo; la giacca → la compro. Before a finite verb, but attached to the infinitive in patterns such as posso comprarla; la posso comprare is also possible. English object pronouns usually follow the verb. Urdu object marking and word order differ: “میں اسے پڑھتا ہوں” corresponds in meaning to I read it but not Italian placement. Check: la giacca, posso cambiar___ → la. Fresh i libri → li leggo. Compare più comodo di …, meno caro di …; context can change comparative patterns, so do not prescribe di for every comparison. Indirect gli/le and combined forms need careful referents.

grammar.title: Conditional requests and advice
grammar.html: Vorrei, potrei, sarebbe, consiglierei soften or frame requests/advice: “Potrei venire alle dieci?” English could/would is a useful meaning bridge, not a full conjugation system. Urdu “کیا میں آ سکتا ہوں؟” or “بہتر ہوگا” can express permission/advice with different wording and agreement. “Sarebbe meglio controllare” — It would be better to check. Check: make Voglio un appuntamento more polite → Vorrei un appuntamento. Fresh request use potere, io → Potrei …? Conditional does not always mean politeness; it also expresses hypothetical results or reported unconfirmed information. Keep those later uses distinct. Directness is contextual; a conditional alone cannot make every message considerate.

grammar.title: Relative clauses, ci and ne
grammar.html: “Il rubinetto che perde acqua” — the tap that leaks. Che can link noun information in common subject/object roles; not all relative relations use che. Ci/ne have several functions; teach limited patterns: ci sono; Ho due libri, ne leggo uno = I read one of them. English there/of them are clues, not consistent replacements. Urdu relative patterns such as “جو کتاب …” use their own structure; translating جو to che everywhere will fail. Check: Ho tre documenti. Ne porto due — how many? two of the three. Fresh relative: the book I read → il libro che leggo. Later cui with a preposition requires separate attention.

grammar.title: Connectors, cause and concession
grammar.html: E/ma/poi link simple ideas; perché gives a reason; tuttavia introduces contrast; benché/sebbene commonly take subjunctive. English because/however/although give functions but not Italian mood requirements. Urdu “کیونکہ” and “اگرچہ” signal related relations with different syntax. “Studio perché voglio capire” — I study because I want to understand; “Benché sia tardi, continuiamo” — Although it is late, we continue. Check: choose perché/tuttavia for “I study __ I want to understand” → perché. Fresh contrast: costs more, however saves travel → Costa di più; tuttavia riduce il viaggio. A connector cannot repair a missing logical link. Don't overuse them as decoration.

grammar.title: Subjunctive frames and sequence
grammar.html: “Penso che sia utile”; “Voglio che venga”; “Benché sia tardi”. Subjunctive relates to constructions, stance and clause relations, not a single “uncertainty tense”. English often uses indicative where Italian uses subjunctive; Urdu clauses with “کہ” also do not determine the Italian mood. “Pensavo che fosse utile” shifts to a past viewpoint; “Pensavo che avesse finito” places completion before that belief. Check: Penso che ___ utile → sia. Fresh past: Pensavo che ___ utile → fosse. Non penso che sia … is a useful negative frame. Reported fact and purpose, register and intended meaning matter; do not change every che clause automatically.

grammar.title: Infinitive, purpose and complements
grammar.html: “Studio per comunicare”; “Imparo a scrivere”; “Cerco di capire”. Different verbs select different complement patterns. English to cannot reliably choose Italian a/di/per. Urdu often expresses purpose through forms such as “سمجھنے کے لیے” (in order to understand), with a different order. “Per capire, faccio domande” — To understand, I ask questions. Check: Imparo ___ scrivere → a; cerco ___ capire → di. Fresh purpose: Studio ___ lavorare meglio → per. Learn the governing verb with its complement. Where subjects differ, a finite clause may be required; purpose clauses with affinché and subjunctive belong to later study, not word-for-word substitution.

grammar.title: Reporting and attribution
grammar.html: “Secondo il comunicato …”; “L'autrice sostiene che …”; “Il documento non conferma …”. Source marking separates your claim from another person's. English according to/reports/argues are functionally useful; Urdu “کے مطابق” or “کہتے ہیں کہ” has its own order and register. “Dice che partirà” versus “Ha detto che sarebbe partito” illustrates a reported future from a past frame; temporal meaning matters more than mechanical tense shifting. Check: rewrite a source claim without endorsing it → Secondo la fonte, … . Fresh identify whether “dice” establishes truth → no. Attribution can still misrepresent scope; preserve quantifiers and conditions, not just a source name.

grammar.title: Real and unreal conditions
grammar.html: “Se piove, resto/resterò a casa.” Hypothetical present: “Se avessi tempo, studierei.” Unreal past: “Se avessi avuto tempo, avrei studiato.” English if/would forms have similarities but different morphology. Urdu “اگر میرے پاس وقت ہوتا …” expresses a hypothetical relation without directly supplying Italian moods. Check: Se avessi tempo, ___ di più → studierei. Fresh unreal past with finire: Se avessi studiato, avrei finito (given intended meaning). Do not put the conditional mechanically after se in these target patterns. Other se constructions exist, including indirect questions, so “conditional can never follow se anywhere” is too broad. Preserve actual versus counterfactual meaning.

grammar.title: Information structure and argument
grammar.html: “Non è il costo in sé a preoccupare, ma la sua distribuzione” foregrounds a contrast. “La proposta, pur interessante, resta incompleta” compresses concession. English clefts and Urdu emphasis through particles/order can express related focus, but cannot prescribe Italian wording. “È questo il punto” — This is the point. Check: what is contrasted in the cost sentence? total cost versus distribution, with concern on the latter. Fresh recast neutrally → Preoccupa come viene distribuito il costo. Distinguish evidence, warrant, inference and limitation. These are discourse choices, not a requirement to make sentences longer. Nominalisation can compress or conceal actors; choose by purpose.

grammar.title: Passive and impersonal constructions
grammar.html: “I dati sono/vengono controllati da un addetto” focuses on data; “Un addetto controlla i dati” names the actor early. “Si lavora qui” is impersonal; “Si controllano i dati” is a passive-si pattern with plural agreement. English passive/one/people and Urdu passive “جانچ کی جاتی ہے” are meaning bridges, not interchangeable syntax. Check: convert Un addetto controlla i dati → I dati vengono controllati da un addetto. Fresh choose singular/plural Si controlla/controllano i documenti → controllano. Passive is not automatically formal excellence. For task instructions, identify who must act. Other pronominal si uses are distinct; avoid treating every si as impersonal.

grammar.title: Scope, register and pragmatic meaning
grammar.html:
“Non tutti hanno approvato” does not mean nobody approved; “Non risulta approvato” does not establish rejection. “Forse potremmo chiarire” may soften a serious concern. English hedges/quantifiers have related functions; Urdu “سب نے منظوری نہیں دی” can also require context to clarify scope, so paraphrase explicitly rather than assume identical ambiguity. Italian example: “Alcuni non hanno approvato; non sappiamo quanti siano favorevoli” — Some did not approve; we do not know how many favour it. Check: does non escluso mean proven? no. Fresh make tentative interpretation → Potrebbe indicare una riserva; occorre verificarlo. Irony and intention require context and sometimes prosody; text alone cannot prove speaker intent.

Worked grammar feedback and fresh transfer

Original: “Lei ho un libro e lei e qui.” Intended meaning: she has a book and she is here. Minimal correction: “Lei ha un libro e lei è qui.” Natural alternative: “Ha un libro ed è qui.” Explain ha for third-person possession and è for is; subject omission is optional. Targeted repair: Sara ___ una penna; Sara ___ a casa. Key ha/è. Fresh task: write about Omar's identity and possession using different nouns. Record person, meaning and spelling separately. Do not add pronouns to every correct Italian sentence or remove them when they are needed for contrast.

units.title: Hello, my name is …
units.html:
Goal: greet, introduce and spell a name. Prerequisite: none. Grammar: G01 address, G02 essere. Words: il nome — name; il corso — course; la penna — pen; grazie — thank you. Visual: scene-board panels 1/3; vocabulary cards 5/9.

Read/listening script

Receptionist: Buongiorno. Come si chiama? Learner: Mi chiamo Amal. E Lei? Receptionist: Mi chiamo Elena. Piacere. Learner: Piacere. Come si scrive Elena? Receptionist: E, L, E, N, A. Learner: Grazie. Arrivederci.

Meaning: the receptionist asks the learner's name; the learner asks for Elena's spelling. E Lei? = And you? politely. Piacere = pleased to meet you.

Explain/example: use Come si chiama? in a polite exchange, Come ti chiami? with someone using tu. Model: friendly partner “Ciao, come ti chiami?” → “Mi chiamo Nora.” Hear vowels in names and spell with Italian letter names; do not use English “eye” for i.

Guided: 1. Who is Elena? 2. Complete Mi ___ Amal. 3. Choose ti/si in the receptionist's question. Independent writing: write a greeting and fictional name for another receptionist. Speaking: ask your partner's name, then request spelling; partner chooses a new name.

Key: 1 receptionist; 2 chiamo; 3 si. Accept Buongiorno. Mi chiamo [name] for writing. Fresh exit: introduce yourself to an informal classmate, switching register. Feedback: meaning, name chunk, register and articulation are separate. Memory: greet → name → spelling → thanks. Word curiosity: ciao's history is in the original pack; historical meaning does not determine modern register.

units.title: I am here; I have a book
units.html:
Goal: distinguish essere/avere by meaning and person. Prerequisite: A1.1. Grammar: G02/G03. Words: il libro — book; l'ufficio — office; una domanda — a question; qui — here; fame — hunger. Visual: be/have decision tree.

Text/script: Sono Amal. Sono in ufficio. Ho un libro e una penna. Elena è qui. Ha una domanda. Io ho fame. Elena ha trent'anni. Non sono Elena: sono Amal.

Meaning: Amal gives identity, location and possessions; Elena has a question and is thirty. Non sono = I am not. The last contrast prevents confusing the speaker with Elena.

Explain/example: first choose meaning, then person. “I have a pen” → possession → avere → io ho → Ho una penna. “She is here” → location → essere → lei è → Lei è qui. Age and hunger use taught avere expressions even when English uses be. Urdu comparison and full forms are in G02/G03 and the original repair lessons.

Guided: 1. Is Amal Elena? 2. Io ___ in ufficio: sono/ho. 3. Elena ___ una domanda: è/ha. 4. I am hungry: Sono/Ho fame. Independent writing: two true or invented sentences, one about where you are and one possession. Speaking: receptionist asks Lei è Amal? and Lei ha un libro? Give complete responses.

Key: 1 no; 2 sono; 3 ha; 4 Ho. Model Sono a casa. Ho un libro. Fresh exit: supplied appointment noun un appuntamento; “I have an appointment” → Ho un appuntamento. “She is at home” → È a casa. Repair: person errors need io/Lei contrast; meaning errors need have/be contrast. Chant: Sono qui. Ho un libro. Lei è qui. Ha un libro. Say naturally, not as a pronunciation score.

units.title: A café order and the bill
units.html:
Goal: choose an item, request politely and understand an invented price. Prerequisite: A1.2; numbers staged with the number clinic. Grammar: G04 articles; G05 number contexts. Words: il caffè — coffee; l'acqua — water; il pane — bread; il conto — bill. Visual: café panel and number-context diagram.

Menu: Caffè €1,50. Acqua €1,00. Pane €2,00. These are teaching prices.

Script: Customer: Buongiorno. Vorrei un caffè e un'acqua, per favore. Staff: Due euro e cinquanta. Customer: Può ripetere? Staff: Due euro e cinquanta. Customer: Grazie.

Explain/example: vorrei is a fixed polite request now, with its conditional grammar later. Un caffè but un'acqua: the feminine una becomes un' before a vowel. Masculine un has no apostrophe, e.g. un amico. Work with a few noun pairs at a time. Model menu: one water → un'acqua → one euro.

Guided: 1. What is ordered? 2. What total is spoken? 3. Correct un acqua. 4. Say €2,00 as a price. Independent: write a different two-item order and calculate from the menu. Role-play: staff changes one item; customer asks for repetition before agreeing.

Key: coffee and water; €2,50; un'acqua; due euro. Example bread + water = €3,00. Fresh exit: coffee alone and a polite thanks. Feedback: check order and amount before spelling details; independent pronunciation needs audio review. Culture: use the particular menu and ingredient information rather than assuming all cafés offer the same food. Memory: noun with article + order chunk + price context.

units.title: People and a small home
units.html:
Goal: describe simple people/room facts. Prerequisite: A1.3, essere/avere. Grammar: G04 agreement; G06 possessives/existentials. Words: la casa, la camera — room; il tavolo — table; il fratello — brother; piccolo/piccola — small.

Text/script: Questa è la mia casa. È piccola. C'è una camera e c'è una cucina. In cucina ci sono due sedie e un tavolo. Mio fratello si chiama Sami. Ha una camera piccola. La sua camera è qui.

Gloss: cucina = kitchen; sedie = chairs; suo/sua = his/her by context. Questa è = this is. Picture claims here are invented, not facts about the generated scene.

Explain/example: c'è introduces one thing; ci sono several. Model: one table → C'è un tavolo; two chairs → Ci sono due sedie. Adjectives agree: camera piccola, tavolo piccolo. Mio fratello commonly omits the article in this singular family pattern; la mia casa keeps it. Do not generalise omission to every family expression.

Guided: 1. How many chairs? 2. ___ due sedie: c'è/ci sono. 3. camera piccolo/piccola. Independent writing: three sentences about an invented room with a supplied list: un tavolo, due sedie, una finestra (window). Speaking: ask Dov'è il tavolo? and answer using a picture you can see.

Key: two; ci sono; piccola. Model Nella camera c'è un tavolo. Ci sono due sedie. C'è una finestra. Fresh exit: one chair becomes two tables; use ci sono due tavoli. Visual task: draw a rough room plan, label actual objects, then hide labels for recall. Culture: home/family structures vary; fictional details are welcome.

units.title: A workday, a class day, a shop day
units.html:
Goal: describe a short routine and time. Prerequisite: A1.4 and clock numbers. Grammar: G07 present; G08 reflexives/time. Words: lavorare — work; studiare — study; aprire — open; iniziare — start; ogni giorno — every day.

Text/script: Amal lavora in ufficio. Inizia alle nove e finisce alle cinque. Sara studia italiano. La lezione inizia alle dieci. Omar ha un negozio. Apre alle otto. Ogni giorno si alza alle sette. Oggi il negozio è chiuso.

Gloss: finisce = finishes; si alza = gets up; chiuso = closed; oggi = today. The schedule is fictional. Finire is an -isc family verb; do not infer that every -ire verb is identical.

Explain/example: parlare → parlo/parli/parla; dormire → dormo; capire → capisco. Model subject change: Amal lavora → Io lavoro. Reflexive io mi alzo / Omar si alza; introduce as one pattern. At nine = alle nove; at one = all'una.

Guided: 1. Who opens at eight? 2. Io lavorare → ___. 3. La lezione inizia ___ dieci. Independent writing: choose worker, student or owner and write three simple routine sentences with changed times. Speaking: A che ora inizi? — At what time do you start? Partner replies and asks back.

Key: Omar; lavoro; alle. Accept a meaningful first-person routine; check the person form separately from the time. Fresh exit: supplied noi + studiare → Studiamo italiano alle nove. Pronunciation: listen for stress in lavoro/lavoriamo after a model; written form does not assess it. Culture discussion: compare this invented routine with your own; avoid assuming a universal Italian lunch break.

units.title: Find the station
units.html:
Goal: locate a place, follow simple directions and ask about departure. Prerequisite: A1.5. Grammar: G09 prepositions/instructions. Words: la stazione — station; il treno — train; a destra — right; a sinistra — left; dritto — straight.

Script: Visitor: Scusi, dov'è la stazione? Local: È vicino. Vada dritto e poi a destra. Visitor: A destra? Local: Sì. Visitor: Grazie. At the station: Un biglietto per Bari, per favore. A che ora parte il treno? Staff: Alle quattordici.

Explain/example: a Bari for city destination; in Italia for country; per Bari in a ticket request. Do not translate every English “to” with the same Italian preposition. Vada dritto is a polite direction chunk; informal vai dritto is another form. Model map: start at café, one turn right → Vada dritto, poi a destra.

Guided: 1. Which turn follows straight? 2. When does the train depart? 3. Un biglietto ___ Bari: per/di. Independent: draw a tiny map with a station, café and one junction. Write two directions, with a legend. Speaking: ask for a ticket to a different supplied city and confirm a new time.

Key: right; 14:00; per. Map answers depend on the learner's drawing; verify the stated route against it. Fresh exit: listener hears a sinistra and selects the left arrow, using genuine audio or leaving listening unassessed. Visual: station scene for observation; never pretend the generated board's small marks are real departure data. Useful phrase: Scusi — Excuse me, politely.

units.title: An appointment and a request for help
units.html:
Goal: arrange/confirm a simple visit and request clarification. Prerequisite: A1.6, days/months supplied as needed. Grammar: G10 modals; G05 dates. Words: l'appuntamento — appointment; il documento — document; domani — tomorrow; portare — bring.

Message/script: Buongiorno, sono Amal. Ho un appuntamento domani, martedì 12 maggio, alle dieci. Posso venire alle undici? Devo portare un documento? Grazie. Reply: Sì, può venire alle undici. Porti un documento, per favore.

Note: this is a fictional calendar message; no present-year weekday claim is made. Porti is a polite instruction chunk. Explain/example: posso + infinitive = I can/may; devo + infinitive = I must/need to. Model “May I come?” → Posso venire? No extra conjugated verb after posso. Polite Lei può differs from io posso.

Guided: 1. Requested new time? 2. Required item? 3. Devo portare/porto un documento. Independent writing: request a changed time using supplied date/time and ask what to bring. Speaking: staff confirms a different time; repeat it back.

Key: 11:00; a document; portare. Model Posso venire alle nove? Devo portare un documento? Fresh exit: supplied parlare = speak; “Can I speak?” → Posso parlare? Repair: distinguish meaning of can/must, then form. Daily-life link: employee confirms a meeting, student a tutorial, owner a delivery visit. Keep the same language target rather than tripling vocabulary load.

units.title: My first week in a new city
units.html:
Goal: combine familiar information in a form, message and exchange. Prerequisite: A1.1–7. No new tense. Visual: scene board; choose a panel and separate observation from invention.

Text/script: Mi chiamo Farah. Sono di Lahore e abito a Bari. Studio italiano la mattina. Il pomeriggio lavoro in un negozio. Il negozio apre alle tre. Ho una casa piccola vicino alla stazione. Oggi ho un appuntamento alle undici. Non capisco una parola e chiedo: «Può ripetere, per favore?»

Gloss: abito = I live; mattina = morning; pomeriggio = afternoon; una parola = a word. Worked example: extract Nome from Mi chiamo Farah → Farah. Independent form fields use other details: città, attività della mattina, ora dell'appuntamento.

Guided: 1. Which city? 2. Morning activity? 3. Appointment time? Independent writing: a 20–30-word introduction with fictional name, city and routine; word range is a course task choice, not a CEFR rule. Speaking: three turns at a registration desk, then one request for repetition. Memory: retrieve five noun+article pairs without choices; check the backs after answering.

Key: Bari; studies Italian; 11:00. Model message: Buongiorno. Mi chiamo Sami e abito a Roma. Studio italiano la mattina e lavoro il pomeriggio. Ho un appuntamento alle dieci. Accept valid alternatives. Fresh exit next visit: a different person/city/time and an unseen picture. Review: use the A1 check in assessments; do not call one passage a full A1 exam. Listening and spoken criteria stay unassessed until actual audio evidence exists.

units.title: A completed day
units.html:
Goal: relate completed familiar actions. Prerequisite: A1 present/essere/avere. Grammar: G11 passato prossimo. Words: arrivare — arrive; comprare — buy; perdere — lose/miss; la ricevuta — receipt. Visual: tense timeline, shop panel.

Text/script: Ieri Amal è arrivata in centro alle nove. Ha comprato un quaderno per il corso e ha preso un caffè. Al negozio ha chiesto la ricevuta. Poi è andata alla stazione, ma ha perso il treno. Ha telefonato a Sara e ha aspettato il treno successivo. Alla fine è arrivata al corso alle dieci e mezza.

Gloss: ieri = yesterday; quaderno = notebook; successivo = next; alla fine = in the end. Explain/example: ha comprato uses avere + participle; è arrivata uses essere and agreement with Amal. Learn auxiliary with the verb. Model Omar è arrivato, Sara è arrivata. Not every movement verb takes essere: ho camminato.

Guided: 1. What did Amal buy? 2. Why was she later? 3. Sara è arrivato/arrivata. 4. Io ___ comprato: sono/ho. Independent writing: 50–70 words about a fictional completed morning using three actions and a result. Speaking: partner asks Che cosa hai fatto ieri?; answer and ask back. Quiet route: exchange written messages.

Key: notebook; she missed the train; arrivata; ho. Model sentence Ieri ho studiato e poi sono andata al lavoro (adapt speaker agreement). Fresh check: supplied verb visitare with avere; Noi ___ visitato il museo → abbiamo. Word connection: receipt is la ricevuta, not English recipe, which is la ricetta. Culture task: discuss asking for a receipt as a language function; specific tax obligations are outside this lesson.

units.title: A routine interrupted
units.html:
Goal: distinguish past background from a completed event. Prerequisite: A2.1. Grammar: G12 imperfetto. Words: mentre — while; piovere — rain; funzionare — work/function; di solito — usually.

Text/script: Quando abitavo vicino all'università, andavo al corso a piedi. Di solito uscivo alle otto e incontravo un'amica al bar. Un lunedì pioveva molto e l'autobus non arrivava. Mentre aspettavo, Sara mi ha telefonato: il corso era online. Sono tornata a casa e ho acceso il computer. Internet funzionava, per fortuna.

Explain/example: abitavo/andavo describe background or repeated routine; ha telefonato introduces a completed event. Model “I was waiting when the phone rang” → Aspettavo quando il telefono ha suonato. These are viewpoint choices, not a rule that every long action takes imperfetto and every short action passato prossimo.

Guided: 1. How did the speaker usually travel? 2. Why return home? 3. Choose Mentre aspettavo/ho aspettato, Sara mi ha telefonato for ongoing background. Independent: 60–80 words about a routine and one disruption, with a changed setting. Discussion: corporate worker has a cancelled meeting, student an online class, owner a delayed delivery. Use the same tense contrast.

Key: on foot; course was online; aspettavo. Accept other forms if the intended viewpoint and context make sense. Fresh exit: I was studying when Marco arrived → Studiavo quando Marco è arrivato. Memory: one background phrase plus one event phrase, not two isolated tense names. Culture: this is an invented day, not evidence about how Italian universities normally organise teaching.

units.title: Make a plan together
units.html:
Goal: suggest a plan, negotiate timing and state a future intention. Prerequisite: A2.2. Grammar: G13 future; G10 modal review. Words: libero/libera — available; rimandare — postpone; il programma — plan/programme.

Script: Sara: Sabato sei libera? Vorrei visitare il museo. Amal: La mattina lavoro, ma finisco alle due. Possiamo incontrarci alle tre? Sara: Va bene. Comprerò i biglietti domani. Amal: Se piove, prendiamo l'autobus. Sara: Perfetto. Ti scrivo venerdì per confermare.

Explain/example: present can describe a clear arrangement: Sabato lavoro. Future can express intention/prediction: Comprerò i biglietti. Model domani + comprare, io → comprerò. Recognise common irregular stems: sarò, avrò, andrò. Do not convert every future-time sentence mechanically.

Guided: 1. When can Amal meet? 2. Who buys tickets? 3. io + avere future → ___. Independent writing: invite someone, state one constraint and offer another time. Speaking: partner declines the first time politely; agree a second. Supply Ti va di …? = Would you like to …? as an optional chunk.

Key: three; Sara; avrò. Model Sabato lavoro fino alle due. Possiamo incontrarci alle quattro? Fresh exit: new role, owner arranges a supplier meeting on a different day. Visual: calendar slots, labelled fictional; ask what is available before reading a model. Register: a friendly invitation and a client appointment differ in greeting and address. Memory: intention + constraint + alternative + confirmation.

units.title: Choose and return a product
units.html:
Goal: compare two products and make a simple return request. Prerequisite: A2.3. Grammar: G14 object pronouns/comparisons. Words: la taglia — size; stretto — tight; cambiare — exchange/change; costare — cost.

Script: Customer: Ho comprato questa giacca ieri, ma è troppo stretta. Posso cambiarla? Staff: Certo. Ha la ricevuta? Customer: Sì, eccola. La giacca blu costa più di quella verde? Staff: No, costano uguale. Vuole provarla? Customer: Sì, grazie. Questa è più comoda.

Explain/example: giacca is feminine singular → la; cambiare + la → cambiarla. Model libro → lo compro; giacca → la compro. More comfortable = più comoda; compare actual items instead of assuming expensive means better. Store/shop policy in this fictional exchange is not a statement of legal return rights.

Guided: 1. What is wrong? 2. Do the two jackets cost different amounts? 3. la giacca → posso cambiarlo/cambiarla. Independent writing: a three-sentence product query with supplied noun il libro and issue una pagina mancante (a missing page). Speaking: ask for an exchange; staff asks one clarification question.

Key: too tight; no; cambiarla. Model Ho comprato questo libro ieri. C'è una pagina mancante. Posso cambiarlo? Fresh exit: le scarpe → le, Posso cambiarle? after plural form instruction. Feedback: pronoun referent first, then placement. Picture activity: compare two drawn price tags; prices are invented. Word family: comodo → comodità; familiar-looking endings are clues, not automatic translation rules.

units.title: A practical health request
units.html:
Goal: state a simple problem and understand a clear practical instruction. Prerequisite: A2.4. Grammar: G15 conditional requests/imperatives. Words: il mal di gola — sore throat; riposare — rest; la visita — appointment/examination; disponibile — available.

Script: Caller: Buongiorno. Vorrei fissare una visita. Ho mal di gola da due giorni. Receptionist: È disponibile domani alle nove? Caller: Potrei venire alle dieci? Receptionist: Sì. Porti il documento e arrivi dieci minuti prima. Caller: Grazie. Può ripetere l'orario?

This is language practice, not diagnostic or treatment advice. Explain/example: vorrei/potrei soften requests. Model Voglio un appuntamento → Vorrei fissare un appuntamento. Arrivi is a polite instruction; informal arriva differs. For states taught here, ho mal di gola, not sono mal di gola.

Guided: 1. How long has the problem lasted? 2. Agreed time? 3. How early? 4. Make Posso venire? more tentative using potrei. Independent: write a short request for a routine appointment with a supplied problem or nonmedical reason. Speaking: caller repeats date/time to confirm; staff corrects one detail.

Key: two days; 10:00; ten minutes; Potrei venire? Fresh exit: change to an administrative visit and ask what to bring. Pronunciation: practise clear time distinctions with a human model; no invented health urgency from the text. Culture: ask the particular service about process and documents; this imaginary dialogue is not official access guidance.

units.title: A problem at home
units.html:
Goal: describe a household problem and arrange a visit. Prerequisite: A2.5. Grammar: G16 relative che, ci/ne patterns. Words: il rubinetto — tap; perdere acqua — leak; il tecnico — technician; il proprietario — landlord/owner.

Message: Buongiorno, sono Amal, l'inquilina dell'appartamento al secondo piano. Il rubinetto che è in cucina perde acqua. Ho provato a chiuderlo bene, ma il problema continua. Domani sono a casa fino alle dodici. Può mandare un tecnico? In cucina ci sono due rubinetti, ma solo uno perde acqua.

Gloss: inquilina = tenant, feminine; solo uno perde acqua = only one leaks. Explain/example: che links a noun and information: il rubinetto che è in cucina. Ci sono = there are. Ne can refer back to a quantity set; keep the pattern limited: Ho due libri. Ne leggo uno. Do not teach all ci/ne uses at once.

Guided: 1. Which tap? 2. Available until when? 3. Link: Il tecnico arriva domani. Il tecnico ripara il rubinetto → Il tecnico che … . Independent: 60–80-word message about a supplied broken light, una lampada che non funziona. Speaking: arrange a visit and confirm the room.

Key: kitchen tap; noon; e.g. Il tecnico che ripara il rubinetto arriva domani. Fresh exit: Ho tre documenti. Ne porto due = I bring two of them. Review: do not infer repair expertise or rental obligations from a language model. Visual: draw a simple floor plan and mark the stated fault; use labels rather than pretending the illustration shows an invisible leak.

units.title: A shared meal and different habits
units.html:
