Mini-conversations: Customer: “Quanto costa?” — How much is it? Staff: “Tre euro e venti.” — Three euros twenty. Customer: “Grazie.” Phone clarification: “Può ripetere il numero?” — Could you repeat the number? Partner reads only a practice fragment. Meeting: “A che ora?” — At what time? Partner: “Alle dieci.” — At ten.

Quiet route: interpret written numbers only. Audio scripts: record each worked example separately, then the guided/independent and exit numbers in separate files; do not show digits when testing dictation. Picture brief/alt: “The same digits appear on a price tag, a clock and a contact field, each clearly labelled.”

5. Six-minute mini-lesson — Italian, regional Italian and dialects

Prerequisite: none for English explanation; Italian repair phrase can be a survival chunk. Outcome: distinguish three concepts and ask for clearer Italian respectfully.

Explain, 2 minutes: standard Italian is the shared learning target. Regional Italian is Italian with regional pronunciation and sometimes vocabulary or grammar features. Many varieties called Italian “dialects”, such as Neapolitan and Sicilian, have their own histories and systems; they are not simply careless or incorrect standard Italian. Some local Romance varieties developed alongside the variety that became standard Italian, rather than descending from today's standard. Italy also has minority languages. These labels involve history, identity and social context; understanding one local variety is not guaranteed by A1 Italian. Treccani: dialetto, historical explanation.

Worked example: someone speaks otherwise recognisable Italian with a different accent. That can be regional Italian; accent difference alone does not prove they are speaking a separate dialect.

Practise, 2 minutes: classify: (1) familiar Italian with a different local pronunciation; (2) a local variety with its own grammar and vocabulary; (3) neutral shared Italian used in a beginner recording. Key: regional Italian; local dialect/variety (precise naming depends on the community); standard Italian. Audio is not supplied, so this is a concept check, not a dialect-identification test.

Phrase and exchange, 1 minute: “Può parlare più lentamente, per favore?” — Could you speak more slowly, please? Partner: “Sì.” Learner: “Grazie.” Avoid telling people their language is bad Italian. A later locally reviewed phrase is “Come si dice in italiano?” — How do you say it in Italian?

Exit, 1 minute: explain in English why a dialect is not merely a wrong accent; then choose the slow-speech request for a new unfamiliar conversation. Accept a meaning-based explanation. Quiet route: write the request. Asset brief: map with several overlapping language areas, captioned “illustrative, not exact borders”; production requires specialist source review. No regional imitation audio is authored yet.

6. Informal, slang and teenager vocabulary

This is recognition-first enrichment for an adult course, not a separate teenage audience. Social words change rapidly; check again before release. “Attested in a source” does not establish popularity among teenagers in October 2026. Offer neutral equivalents for work and formal encounters.

Expression Meaning and register Neutral/polite alternative Source/status
Boh I don't know / uncertainty; informal, may sound dismissive by tone Non lo so — I don't know Treccani; established colloquial item, not teenager-only
Ci becchiamo See you / catch up; colloquial peer use Ci vediamo; in a polite farewell, arrivederci Crusca youth-language volume; attested, not a claim of current universal use
Cringe Embarrassing/awkward in internet/peer contexts Imbarazzante Crusca entry; source is historical attestation; current frequency not measured
Che figo! / Che fico! Roughly “How cool!”; very informal, can carry coarse associations Che bello! — How nice/great! Crusca discussion; teach recognition and register before optional use

Worked register choice: client asks a question you cannot answer. Prefer “Non lo so” with a helpful continuation at your later level, rather than an isolated “Boh”. Check: (1) staff registration goodbye: arrivederci or ci becchiamo? (2) an informal friend chat: can cringe be encountered? Key: arrivederci; yes, but recognise context rather than assuming every young person uses it. Fresh transfer: rewrite “Ci becchiamo” for a formal departure → Arrivederci. Regional slang collections remain a research task until a destination is known.

7. Seven daily curiosity, culture and rhythm cards

Read one word/history fact and one culture observation per day in English, 30–60 seconds total. The chants are original memory lines written for this project; they are rhythmic practice, not every line a rhyme or a traditional Italian song. Use a natural spoken beat or a newly composed melody. Do not attach a copyrighted tune. They do not replace ordinary conversational stress models. A teacher must check any produced recording.

Day Word/letter curiosity and culture note Original memory chant with English meaning Link to the lesson
D01 Ciao has a Venetian history related to a deferential “your servant/slave” formula; its ordinary modern use is friendly hi/bye, not that literal historical meaning. Treccani. Notice how greeting register depends on the relationship, not a claim that all adults greet the same way. “Ciao, ciao! Mi chiamo Sara. / Buongiorno! Mi chiamo Sara.” — Hi, hi! My name is Sara. / Good morning/day! My name is Sara. Choose the greeting; substitute a name.
D02 Alfabeto, like English alphabet, refers to Greek alpha and beta. B has a history through Greek beta and an earlier Phoenician letter name associated with house; English B and Italian B share letter ancestry, not identical spoken names. Alphabet, beta. Names may come from many languages; do not “Italianise” someone's name without asking. “Emme, i, a: Mia! / Elle, i, a: Lia!” — M-I-A: Mia; L-I-A: Lia. Letter names, not letter sounds.
D03 H once represented an aspirated sound in Latin; Italian h in ho/ha is now silent and remains useful in spelling. English h often has a sound, so the same letter does not imply the same pronunciation. Treccani h. Religion/culture: Italy has diverse religious and nonreligious lives; constitutional Article 8 concerns religious freedom. Learn customs without assigning beliefs to an individual. Senate. “Come ti chiami? Mi chiamo Ali. / Come si chiama? Mi chiamo Ali.” — Informal/polite name question; my name is Ali. Hear the register change; h fact is a preview only.
D04 Caffè reached Italian through Turkish kahve from Arabic qahwa. A word can travel across languages without carrying exactly the same modern form. Treccani. Food practice: read the actual menu and ask what an unfamiliar dish contains; never infer ingredients from a romantic name or regional stereotype. “Caffè, per favore. / Grazie, grazie.” — Coffee, please. / Thank you, thank you. Coffee word, polite request. Per favore is previewed here and core on D05.
D05 Doppio comes from Latin duplus; connect the idea of “double” with the two written letters, but listen for sound duration. Treccani. Holiday note: Ferragosto is 15 August; it sits in the summer holiday season. Ask about a particular business's hours rather than assuming everything closes. Official tourism page is a 2025 example, not a verified 2026 opening-hours calendar. “La pala, la palla. / La pala, la palla.” — The shovel, the ball, repeated. Keep natural word stress and a clear longer l; rhyme does not prove perception.
D06 Famiglia comes from Latin familia; the ordinary modern translation is family. Learn la famiglia, not an invented English-suffix conversion. Treccani. Family customs and structures vary: ask who someone lives with rather than assuming a single model of Italian family life. “Il pane, la pasta. / Il caffè, la casa.” — The bread, the pasta; the coffee, the house. Article+noun pairs; these two lines are a memory list, not a sentence about eating a house.
D07 Scuola comes through Latin schola from Greek scholē, historically connected with leisure devoted to learning. English school is a useful cognate, not proof that spelling/sounds match. Treccani. History note: Republic Day on 2 June commemorates the 1946 choice of a republic. Senate. “Mi chiamo Amal. Sono di Bari. / Piacere, piacere!” — My name is Amal. I am from Bari. Pleased to meet you. Write and say an introduction with new facts.

Daily check: ask one meaning question, not a trivia exam: “How would this fact help you remember today's phrase?” Facts and chants must not be prerequisites for advancing the core skill.

Later culture rotation, outlined: M2 local foods/menu ingredients and coffee practices; M3 family forms and invitations; M4 daily routines without assuming a universal lunch break; M5 markets and shopping customs; M6 city history and public-space etiquette; M7 regional travel and local patron-saint days; M8 neighbours/shared housing; M9 workplace register; M10 appointment etiquette; M11 Christmas, Easter and local festivals alongside minority-faith and secular practices. Before release, verify dates, religious explanations, regional practices and exact sites. For churches, mosques or other religious sites, check that venue's visitor rules instead of generalising. No learner is expected to practise a religion or consume a particular food/drink.

8. Daily discussion — corporate worker, student, business owner

Use the same learning target through three adult identities. A learner chooses one each day or alternates. Week 1 uses the accessible prompt only; later Italian expansions are clearly gated until their vocabulary/grammar has been taught. Role-play facts are invented, not claims about all Italians. English reflection is allowed before the Italian turns.

Day/theme Corporate worker prompt Student prompt Business-owner prompt Week 1 model / later expansion
D01 arrival Greet reception on your first workday Greet your course reception Greet a new customer “Buongiorno. Mi chiamo Amal.” Later M1: Sono in ufficio — I am in the office.
D02 details Spell your name for a visitor pass Spell your name for enrolment Spell your name for a supplier contact “Come si scrive? / A, L, I.” Later M1: provide fictional contact fields.
D03 relationships Ask a new client their name politely Ask a course partner using tu Ask a new supplier politely “Come si chiama?” / “Come ti chiami?” Change context, not just a name.
D04 clarification You miss a colleague's coffee question You miss the café staff's question You miss a customer's word “Può ripetere?” Later M9: specify the misunderstood instruction.
D05 request Ask for coffee during a break Ask for coffee between classes Ask for coffee before opening “Caffè, per favore.” Later M2: order and confirm price; M4: say when the break is.
D06 selection Choose bread/pasta in a work canteen Choose bread/pasta at a café Label two food items in a shop “La pasta, per favore” / labels il pane, la pasta. Later M5: quantities and prices.
D07 introduction Write a brief introduction to a new team Write to your new study group Write a brief personal introduction to a business contact “Buongiorno. Mi chiamo Amal. Sono di Lahore.” Later M9: add role and availability.

After M4, a complete 3-minute discussion card:

Glossary: lavoro = I work; studio = I study; apro = I open; un negozio = a shop; alle nove = at nine; alle otto = at eight; alle dieci = at ten. Teach these before asking for independent use.

  • Worker model: “Lavoro in ufficio. Inizio alle nove.” — I work in an office. I start at nine.
  • Student model: “Studio italiano. Inizio alle otto.” — I study Italian. I start at eight.
  • Owner model: “Ho un negozio. Apro alle dieci.” — I have a shop. I open at ten.
  • Partner asks: “A che ora?” — At what time? Learner answers with a changed time.

Guided: choose a role and complete one model with a supplied time. Independent: switch role and time with the model hidden; say two sentences. Feedback: did role and time make sense? Was the first-person form correct? Fresh check next visit: give a different role and start time. Quiet route: a two-sentence message; S/L remain unassessed. Do not turn this into an unscaffolded interview about corporate strategy at A1.

9. Memory flashcards and grammar-confirmation checks

These are actual text card fronts/backs, ready for content review. No interactive flashcard system has been built. Show the front alone; reveal the back after a response. Start with 3 cards, later 5, and follow the review schedule. Ask for a fresh sentence after recall rather than treating recognition as mastery.

ID / prerequisite Front Back / acceptable response Evidence
F01 / D01 You greet an adult receptionist during the day Buongiorno Context → recall
F02 / D01 Give your name without a model Mi chiamo [name]; Sono [name] valid if known Independent chunk use
F03 / D01 Someone hands you a visitor card; thank them Grazie Function → recall
F04 / D02 Spell Sara with Italian letter names esse–a–erre–a Letter-name recall; spoken only if actually spoken
F05 / D03 Ask a friendly classmate's name using tu Come ti chiami? Register + form
F06 / D03 Ask an unfamiliar receptionist's name politely Come si chiama? Register + form
F07 / D04 You did not understand a staff member Può ripetere? Repair phrase
F08 / D04 Predict the initial c in supplied word cane /k/ Sound–spelling prediction, not actual pronunciation
F09 / D05 Say please Per favore Recall
F10 / D05 Hidden audio says palla: choose ball or shovel Ball; do not show the transcript on the front Listening; unavailable until audio is produced
F11 / D06 Complete ___ casa la casa Article recognition; choices optional
F12 / D06 New bread picture, no written cue il pane Recall; picture not yet produced
F13 / D07 I am from Bari Sono di Bari Chunk recall
F14 / EA1 I have a book Ho un libro Meaning → form
F15 / EA1 She is here Lei è qui Meaning + person
F16 / EA1 She has a book Lei ha un libro Meaning + person
F17 / EA1 I am hungry Ho fame Fixed expression
F18 / EA1 I am twenty Ho vent'anni Fixed expression
F19 / EA1 We are here Siamo qui Person transfer
F20 / EA1 They have a book Hanno un libro Person transfer
F21 / EA2 Correct: Sara e qui Sara è qui Orthography; distinguish and/is
F22 / EA2 Correct: Sara a un libro Sara ha un libro Orthography; ha/a
F23 / M4 We speak: parlare, noi parliamo Conjugation
F24 / M4 They sleep: dormire, loro dormono Conjugation
F25 / M4 I understand: capire, io capisco -isc family
F26 / word patterns Slowly; supplied adjective lento lentamente Word formation
F27 / word patterns Family, noun, with article la famiglia False-pattern repair
F28 / M2 prices €3,50: read as a price tre euro e cinquanta centesimi; tre e cinquanta valid in clear context Numeric context
F29 / M1 digits 004 as a code fragment zero zero quattro Identifier vs quantity
F30 / dialect mini-lesson Is a dialect simply badly spoken standard Italian? Why? No; local varieties may have distinct histories and systems Concept check, not proficiency score

Grammar-confirmation check A — after EA1/EA2, not Week 1

Task-format model: “I have a pen” → Ho una penna; avere for possession, io → ho. New assessed items use different meanings/persons.

  1. I am in the office: Io ___ in ufficio.
  2. You have a question, polite: Lei ___ una domanda.
  3. They are here: Loro ___ qui.
  4. We have a book: Noi ___ un libro.
  5. She is hungry: Lei ___ fame.
  6. Choose: “Sara è qui e Ali ha un libro” or “Sara e qui è Ali a un libro”.
  7. Explain why “Ho vent'anni” uses ho even though English says “I am twenty”.
  8. Explain the difference between “Lei è qui” and “Lei ha un libro”.

Key: 1 sono; 2 ha; 3 sono; 4 abbiamo; 5 ha; 6 first sentence; 7 Italian age expression uses avere, subject io gives ho; 8 being/location versus possession, both third-person singular. Accept meaning-equivalent explanations in English. Correct answers without explanations support performance on these items; explanations help diagnose whether the rule is understood.

Repair: errors 1/5/7 → meaning contrast; 2/3/4 → person table; 6 → spelling e/è/a/ha; 8 → compare two pictures, being somewhere versus having an object. Do not declare overall grammar mastered from eight questions.

Fresh check B, next visit: 1. You are here, informal: Tu ___ qui. 2. I have a question: Io ___ una domanda. 3. They have a book: Loro ___ un libro. 4. She is in the office: Sara ___ in ufficio. 5. Explain one choice. Key: sei; ho; hanno; è; explanation states meaning and subject. Use a later changed-context check for retention.

Later-library integration

Add one word-family/cognate card, one fact/culture note, one original chant or reviewed media slice, three flashcards and one grammar transfer check to each authored lesson as optional linked content. Keep workplace/student/owner versions attached to one core target, rather than duplicating entire courses. Complete future-module fact cards, destination-specific dialect examples and vetted song timestamps during authoring; they are not yet a finished 84-day enrichment library.

The Italian Experiment — linked beginner companion

Requested reference incorporated on 19 October 2026. The publisher's beginner lesson index and fifteen linked lesson pages were inspected. They are useful supplementary beginner references, not an A1–C2 curriculum. Public text pages were accessible; audio links were visible, but playback, offline rights and regional availability were not tested. Internet is required to use the linked site. Advertised free lessons do not establish a licence to copy its text, illustrations or recordings.

This file contains direct source links and independently authored practice, not a local reproduction or close rewrite of the publisher's lessons. No page text, audio, image, proverb collection or story has been bundled. Our exercises use adult work/study/business situations and link to the course's own grammar diagrams and flashcards.

Where the references fit

Months A1.7 IE03

How to use a reference without making it an assessment answer

Study the small topic in our course, optionally open the matching reference, and then return with its page closed. Attempt a changed-context task below. If the source remains visible, record support. Use only 3–5 minutes of optional reference work in a normal visit; don't read fifteen lessons at once. These are mini-drills, not fifteen complete mixed-skill daily lessons. The shared grammar cards contain English/Urdu comparisons and their limits.

IE01 — Which job is the number doing?

New teaching point: a quantity, price and identifier need different readings. Model: 15 notebooks → quindici quaderni; code fragment 015 → zero uno cinque. The code is not a phone number to call.

Guided: say 12 as a quantity, then 012 as a code. Independent: an invented price tag shows €4,50; give the price, then write a polite request for one coffee. Key: dodici; zero uno due; quattro euro e cinquanta centesimi; Un caffè, per favore. Fresh check: €6,20, with the diagram hidden → sei euro e venti centesimi. Memory: A1-13/14 and number-context visual. A correct number response does not establish actual listening unless a recording was heard.

IE02 — A day versus a recurring day

Point: lunedì can refer to Monday in context; il lunedì commonly means on Mondays. Names: lunedì, martedì, mercoledì, giovedì, venerdì, sabato, domenica. Use lower case unless sentence position requires a capital. Model: Il lunedì studio — I study on Mondays; Lunedì ho una visita — I have an appointment on Monday.

Guided: choose a recurring study day. Independent: write one routine and one appointment with different days. Key model: Il martedì lavoro in ufficio. Giovedì ho un appuntamento. Other choices accepted. Fresh: partner supplies Wednesday; ask whether they are available. Model Sei libero/libera mercoledì? Memory: create a new routine card using your own schedule, without a notification system.

IE03 — Month names in a date

Point: gennaio, febbraio, marzo, aprile, maggio, giugno, luglio, agosto, settembre, ottobre, novembre, dicembre. Learn in small calendar groups, not all as one exit requirement. Model: La visita è il 14 giugno — The appointment is on 14 June. Il primo maggio uses the ordinal primo for the first day; ordinary later dates use cardinals.

Guided: supplied 12/09 → il dodici settembre. Independent: write two fictional appointment dates, with no weekday claim unless a calendar is checked. Key: dates correctly paired with months; no automatic day/month reversal. Fresh: 03/11 in Italian notation → il tre novembre. Memory: place date cards on a paper calendar; this is a lesson aid, not an alarm or reminder.

IE04 — Article families, one small set at a time

Point: masculine examples il libro/i libri, lo zaino/gli zaini, l'ufficio/gli uffici; feminine la casa/le case, l'aula/le aule. Do not teach endings as exception-free gender rules. Model: zaino begins with a pattern selecting lo; plural gli zaini. Full sound conditions are introduced gradually in G04.

Guided: la casa → le case; il libro → i libri. Independent: choose the supplied pair for two offices: gli uffici / le uffici. Key: gli uffici. Fresh: label a new house picture with la casa, then imagine two → le case. Memory: P02/P09; noun and article stay together. If agreement succeeds only with the chart open, record supported evidence.

IE05 — Ask for the missing kind of information

Point: dove asks location, quando time, chi person, perché reason, come manner, quanto amount. Model: response Alle nove → A che ora?; response In ufficio → Dove? A question should fit the information needed.

Guided: supplied reply Mi chiamo Sara → Come ti chiami? informal. Independent: ask the price of a coffee and the location of the station. Key: Quanto costa il caffè? Dov'è la stazione? Fresh: ask when a class starts → A che ora inizia la lezione? Memory: write a question on the front and a type of answer on the back. Do not memorise one response as the answer to every question.

IE06 — A family description without assumptions

Point: la famiglia, il fratello, la sorella, i genitori. Ask about the particular person; fictional families and non-family households are valid. Model: Mia sorella si chiama Hana. Ha una casa piccola — My sister is called Hana. She has a small house.

Guided: brother named Sami → Mio fratello si chiama Sami. Independent: write two sentences about an invented relative or household member; say who they are and one supplied fact. Key: meaningful identity and correct person; do not require a real disclosure. Fresh: change sister to brother and observe mia/mio. Memory: A1-16 and word-family diagram: la famiglia, familiare, la familiarità. English “family” does not turn into an adjective by adding -oso.

IE07 — Follow a small map

Point: a destra, a sinistra, dritto. Model map: start at a café, continue straight to a junction, then left to an office. Polite direction: Vada dritto, poi a sinistra. This invented route is not real navigation advice.

Guided: replace left with right in the model. Independent: draw a new two-step route from a station to a classroom and describe it. Key: Vada dritto, poi a destra for guided; check independent directions against the actual drawing. Fresh: partner gives a new left/right order; follow it only with real spoken input, otherwise mark reading. Memory: separate arrow cards from place-name cards, then combine them.

IE08 — Essere at an office desk

Point: choose person forms after meaning. Model: We are here → location → essere → noi siamo → Siamo qui. Guided: I am at home → Sono a casa. Independent: polite you are here; they are in the office. Key: Lei è qui; Loro sono in ufficio. Fresh: informal you are Sara? → Tu sei Sara?

Use the be/have diagram and A1-06/08. Repair: if you chose ho for location, return to meaning. If you chose sono for polite Lei, repair person. The reference offers another explanation; it is not an assessment key. English/Urdu grammar: G02/G01 explain where be/ہوں/ہے comparisons help and where social/person systems differ.

IE09 — Avere, including hunger and age

Point: possession and the taught fixed expressions select avere. Model: We have a question → Abbiamo una domanda. Guided: I have a pen → Ho una penna. Independent: she is hungry; I am twenty. Key: Ha fame; Ho vent'anni. Fresh: polite you have an appointment? → Lei ha un appuntamento?

Use A1-05/07/09/10 and P05. Grammar confirmation: explain why Lei è is not the equivalent of io ho: it changes both verb and person. Match io ho / Lei ha, and io sono / Lei è. Limit: personal temperature Ho freddo differs from a room description La camera è fredda. No rule that all feelings use avere. Full comparisons are in G03 and the original repair lessons.

IE10 — A regular -are verb at work or class

Point: parlare stem parl- combines with person endings: -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano. Model: noi + parlare → parliamo. Guided: io + studiare → studio. Independent: tu + lavorare; loro + parlare. Key: lavori; parlano. Fresh: voi + studiare → studiate.

Use: write two sentences as a student, then change to a worker. Model Studio italiano. Lavoro in ufficio. Memory: A1-15 and present-tense grid. Regular families are useful, but not every verb ending in -are behaves without spelling/stem changes. Grammar check: identify the subject before choosing an ending; pronoun omission is optional when context is clear.

IE11 — A regular -ere verb in a useful phrase

Point: leggere has present forms leggo, leggi, legge, leggiamo, leggete, leggono. It illustrates a common family, not every irregular -ere verb. Model: noi + leggere → Leggiamo il messaggio — We read the message.

Guided: io + leggere → leggo. Independent: voi + prendere; Sara + leggere. Key: prendete; Sara legge. Fresh: loro + prendere → prendono. Use: ask a partner to say what they read, with supplied noun il documento. Memory: conjugation grid and B1 person-transfer practice; a table response does not prove fluent use. English/Urdu person comparisons and their limits remain in G07 rather than being duplicated.

IE12 — On time, early and late

Point: in orario = on time; in anticipo = early; in ritardo = late. Learn with a clock comparison. Model: appointment 10:00, arrival 09:50 → Sono in anticipo. This is a fictional timing example.

Guided: appointment 10:00, arrival 10:00 → Sono in orario. Independent: arrival 10:15 for the same appointment → Sono in ritardo. Fresh: change both appointment and arrival by a different interval and explain. Role-play: staff asks arrival time; learner apologises if appropriate, without inventing a dramatic excuse. Memory: three clock states, not isolated translation cards. Audio time discrimination still requires actual recordings.

IE13 — Whose thing, and which grammatical agreement?

Point: la sua valigia can mean his or her suitcase; sua agrees with valigia, not the owner's gender. Model: un uomo + la valigia → la sua valigia. Common singular family patterns can omit an article: mia sorella, with limits in G06.

Guided: my house → la mia casa. Independent: his/her book; our house. Key: il suo libro; la nostra casa. Fresh: their books → i loro libri. Loro is invariable here while the article/noun mark plural. Memory: P11 and a changed-context possessive card. Grammar check: explain why il sua libro is mismatched. Urdu comparison in G06 helps notice agreement, without copying genders from one language to another.

IE14 — Agreement carries across a description

Point: un ufficio piccolo, una camera piccola, uffici piccoli, camere piccole. Some adjectives have different ending families; grande → grandi in plural. Model: two small rooms → due camere piccole.

Guided: a small book → un libro piccolo. Independent: two small books; a large room. Key: due libri piccoli; una camera grande. Fresh: two large rooms → due camere grandi. Use: describe three visible or drawn objects; supplied nouns prevent unfamiliar vocabulary from disguising the agreement target. Memory: label ARTICLE / NOUN / ADJECTIVE with text as well as colour. Recognising a coloured pattern is supported practice; retrieve later without it.

IE15 — Adjective position can affect interpretation

Point: adjective placement depends on meaning, idiom and context; “always after the noun” is too strong. Model: un vecchio amico often means a longstanding friend; un amico vecchio typically describes an elderly friend. Context may refine either interpretation.

Guided: choose a phrase for someone you have known for years → un vecchio amico. Independent: explain the likely distinction in English without inventing someone's age. Key: longstanding relationship versus age-focused description; not a promise that every adjective follows this pair's pattern. Fresh: identify whether una casa piccola concerns physical size; yes. Memory: an advanced meaning card, not a requirement for the first beginner week. Revisit later when context-sensitive adjective meaning can be practised with more examples.

Review and rights record

Reference URLs and page access were checked; third-party audio was not downloaded, transcribed or redistributed. External playback is online and subject to publisher conditions. Our 15 companion drills can be read offline because they are original course text. Existing flashcards, diagrams and picture sheets supply local practice. A publisher permission/licence would be needed before bundling its protected materials; no such permission is claimed here.

references.title: Visual workbook
references.html:
Visual workbook — pictures, diagrams and graphs

Two generated illustration sheets and twelve editable diagrams are included. Each diagram has both SVG and PNG. They are original teaching aids. Concept diagrams are not measured progress data, validated causal models or proof of pronunciation. Figures are paired with tasks below so they support retrieval and transfer.

V01 — Everyday adult-life scene board

Six adult scenes: reception, café, study, office, shop delivery and station

Observed layout: 1 reception; 2 café counter with coffee/bread/pasta; 3 adults studying; 4 office interaction; 5 owner/supplier delivery; 6 travellers looking at a station board. Generated details are illustrative, not actual institutions or legible timetable data.

  • A1: choose panel 1; give an appropriate greeting and chosen name. Panel 2: point to coffee/bread/pasta and retrieve article+noun. Model on a different object first: book → il libro.
  • A2: invent a short account of what happened before panel 6; clearly label it imagined. Use three past actions. Don't claim the image itself proves a delay.
  • B1: describe a practical problem in panel 5 and propose two steps; partner asks one clarification.
  • B2: compare worker/student/owner scheduling constraints using panels 3–5; distinguish what you can see from added assumptions.
  • C1: write two notices about the same invented office change, one team-facing and one public, preserving facts across register.
  • C2: analyse what each framing emphasises and omits; offer two plausible readings without inferring nationality, belief or motive from appearance.

Key: there is no unique story. Objective visible objects and register can be checked; invented events must be labelled. Accept alternative valid Italian. Gender/identity/nationality cannot be established solely from the illustration.

V02 — Picture vocabulary and contrast sheet

Twelve numbered objects for vocabulary retrieval

Key: 1 il caffè; 2 la casa; 3 il pane; 4 la pasta; 5 la penna; 6 la palla; 7 la pala; 8 la chiave; 9 il libro; 10 il treno; 11 la valigia; 12 l'orologio (masculine), showing nine o'clock. Backs and printing instructions are in the flashcard bank.

Recognition round: ask for the book, then show choices. Recall round: point to an object, hide choices and ask for article+noun. Spelling round: write a label with the image visible. Use round: new request, e.g. ask for the pen politely. Delayed round: use a different object drawing or real item next visit. Listening round: only after real audio exists, play pala/palla with transcript hidden; picture selection tests the heard contrast. A correct picture label is not pronunciation evidence.

Advanced transfer: explain how a label can change interpretation: la casa can mean house/home, la penna can have other senses, and an image normally selects one sense rather than teaching every one. Ask what context would be needed for translation.

V03 — Whole-course pathway

Conceptual A1 to C2 pathway

Task: match a task to the proposed emphasis: supported introduction, routine past account, developed argument, nuanced mediation. Key: A1, A2, B2, C1 respectively, but actual difficulty depends on task conditions. This is a planning map, not a placement algorithm or timetable. Fresh check: give an example of a person being stronger in reading than speaking.

V04 — Essere or avere decision diagram

Meaning and person decision diagram

Worked example: I have a book → possession → avere → io → ho. Guided: I am here → Sono qui. She has a book → Ha un libro. Independent: polite “You are here”; I am hungry; we have a question. Key: Lei è qui; Ho fame; Abbiamo una domanda. Fresh: supplied un appuntamento → Ho un appuntamento. The diagram covers common beginner meanings; past-tense auxiliary selection is separate.

V05 — Present conjugation grid

Six-person verb reference grid

Task: cover one column and retrieve noi + parlare, io + capire, Lei + avere. Key: parliamo; capisco; ha. Fresh: voi + prendere → prendete. Explain the subject and family before the ending. Knowledge of a table is not independent conversational use. Read a short role-play next and transfer the forms.

V06 — Numbers change jobs

Quantities, prices, codes, time, dates and decimals

Task: say which context requires separate digits and which a money expression. Key: code fragment versus price. Transfer: 005 → zero zero cinque; €3,20 → tre euro e venti centesimi; 15:30 → le quindici e trenta. Teacher supplies actual audio separately for dictation. The pictured prices are invented; date is a notation example, not a scheduled event.

V07 — Tense and possibility timeline

Symbolic tense and mood relationships

Task: distinguish past background, completed event, arrangement, hypothetical present and unreal past. Key examples: studiavo; è arrivata; domani lavoro; se avessi tempo studierei; se avessi avuto tempo avrei studiato. Fresh: move a learner's scenario from real to hypothetical without preserving the same commitment. A timeline is a support, not a duration-only rule.

V08 — Pronoun reference map

Direct object and indirect recipient examples

Task: what changes between la giacca and a Sara? Key: the object purchased versus the recipient written to. Practice: il libro → lo leggo; a Marco → gli scrivo. Fresh: la penna → la compro. The chart deliberately excludes many combined/tonic pronoun cases; don't apply it as the complete system.

V09 — Qualified argument graph

Evidence, limitation, qualified claim and next check

Task: a pilot records more attendance but not learning. Put the actual observation in evidence and the missing outcome in limitation. Key: increased attendance during pilot; no measured learning result/causal comparison. A warranted claim is narrower than “the pilot improves proficiency”. Fresh: use shop transactions instead of attendance. Nodes are conceptual, not a statistical model.

V10 — Register ladder

Same update in formal, team and public wording

Task: identify invariant facts in all three messages. Key: postponed trial, incomplete staffing, no confirmed new date. Fresh: replace the cause with missing equipment while preserving decision status. An effective rewrite changes wording and emphasis but not the commitments.

V11 — Sound–spelling comparison chart

Common c g ch gh sc gn gli and double-consonant examples

Task: sort casa/cena/chiave by consonant pattern, then listen to reviewed examples. Key: /k/, /tʃ/, /k/. Fresh: cane /k/, cinema /tʃ/. Exception-sensitive gn/gli and z remain word-led learning; the examples are not universal claims about every letter sequence. No phonetic rating from a written chart.

V12 — Learning loop

Recall, explanation, practice, independent use, repair and delayed check

Task: does looking at a card establish mastery? Key: no. Transfer: after a successful card, use a new situation and delay the next check. The diagram describes a proposed workflow, not proof of its effectiveness for every learner. Use the quiet route when speaking is impractical.

V13 — Word-family connections

Suffix clues and false-friend examples

Task: translate family and slowly; explain why a suffix guess can fail. Key: la famiglia, lentamente; meanings/stems vary and friendly is not an -ly adverb. Fresh: facile → facilmente, quality → la qualità. Check meanings rather than manufacturing words.

V14 — Evidence lanes

Recognition, listening, recall, spelling and independent-use evidence

Task: a learner chooses a correct meaning but cannot spell the word. Which evidence is present? Key: recognition; spelling needs work. Fresh: learner transcribes a phrase correctly but no expert hears the recording: transcript evidence is available, pronunciation remains unassessed. No filled-in learner scores are invented.

Print and accessibility notes

Open an SVG for editable sharp labels, or use its PNG for broad compatibility. The review book displays PNGs and alt descriptions; headings and text repeat the instructional meaning. Colour is paired with labels. All 12 diagrams are conceptual/static teaching visuals, not fabricated learner performance graphs. Test final print contrast and text sizes on the intended paper before mass printing.

Keep gn together in the written model. Between vowels this consonant is normally long.

Three syllables in this model; lia is not split into li-a.
Stress lia. Do not count every written vowel as a separate beat.
Stress le, not fo. Dictionary stress marks are not normally written in the word.
Five syllables; final stress and written à.
Here a and stressed u are in separate syllables: a hiatus. Vowel pairs are word-specific.
Here o and e form separate syllables. Consult a dictionary for unfamiliar vowel sequences.
Three syllables; double s and first-syllable stress.
Three syllables; middle stress.

cards.front: Greet an adult receptionist during the day.
cards.back: Buongiorno.

cards.front: Introduce yourself with a chosen name.
cards.back: Mi chiamo [name]. Sono [name] is also valid if known.

cards.front: Ask a friendly classmate's name using tu.
cards.back: Come ti chiami?

cards.front: Ask a receptionist's name using polite address.
cards.back: Come si chiama?

cards.front: I have a book. Choose ho or sono.
cards.back: Ho un libro. Avere for possession, io form ho.

cards.front: I am in the office. Choose ho or sono.
cards.back: Sono in ufficio. Essere for this location, io form sono.

cards.front: She has a question. Choose ha or è.
cards.back: Lei ha una domanda. Avere, third-person singular.

cards.front: She is here. Choose ha or è.
cards.back: Lei è qui. Essere, third-person singular.

cards.front: I am hungry.
cards.back: Ho fame. Italian uses this avere expression.

cards.front: I am twenty.
cards.back: Ho vent'anni. Age uses avere.

cards.front: Complete: ___ casa; ___ pane.
cards.back: La casa; il pane. Learn the noun with its article.

cards.front: Please ask a staff member to repeat.
cards.back: Può ripetere, per favore?

cards.front: €2,50 as a price, not a code.
cards.back: Due euro e cinquanta centesimi; due e cinquanta in clear context.

cards.front: Read practice code fragment 004.
cards.back: Zero zero quattro. Preserve leading zeros.

cards.front: We speak: parlare, noi.
cards.back: Parliamo.

cards.front: Family, as a noun with its article.
cards.back: La famiglia. Not an automatic -oso conversion.

cards.front: Sara arrived: Sara è arrivato or arrivata?
cards.back: Sara è arrivata. Essere participle agrees in this example.

cards.front: I bought a notebook yesterday.
cards.back: Ieri ho comprato un quaderno.

cards.front: Background: I was studying when Sara arrived.
cards.back: Studiavo quando Sara è arrivata.

cards.front: Does every movement verb take essere?
cards.back: No. Ho camminato; learn the auxiliary with the verb.

cards.front: Tomorrow I will have time: io + avere future.
cards.back: Domani avrò tempo.

cards.front: A clear future arrangement can use present?
cards.back: Yes: Domani lavoro. Context fixes the arrangement.

cards.front: Replace la giacca: I buy it.
cards.back: La compro.

cards.front: May I exchange it? Object: la giacca.
cards.back: Posso cambiarla? La posso cambiare? also possible.

cards.front: Ask tentatively if you could come at ten.
cards.back: Potrei venire alle dieci?

cards.front: More comfortable, describing a feminine jacket.
cards.back: Più comoda.

cards.front: Link: the tap that leaks.
cards.back: Il rubinetto che perde acqua.

cards.front: Ho tre libri. Ne leggo due. How many read?
cards.back: Two of the three books. Ne refers to the set.

cards.front: We meet one another at seven.
cards.back: Ci incontriamo alle sette.

cards.front: Read 14:30 as clock time.
cards.back: Le quattordici e trenta.

cards.front: Is a fictional shop dialogue proof of return rights?
cards.back: No. It practises language; real policy/law needs its source.

cards.front: Slow → slowly; supplied adjective lento.
cards.back: Lento → lenta → lentamente. Check the exact form.

cards.front: Four steps for a clear incident narrative.
cards.back: Background → disruption → response → result.

cards.front: I would advise trying a lesson.
cards.back: Consiglierei di provare una lezione.

cards.front: Target frame: Penso che ___ utile.
cards.back: Penso che sia utile.

cards.front: I learn to write: imparo ___ scrivere.
cards.back: Imparo a scrivere. Learn the complement with the verb.

cards.front: I try to understand: cerco ___ capire.
cards.back: Cerco di capire.

cards.front: I study in order to communicate.
cards.back: Studio per comunicare.

cards.front: If it rains, we will stay home. Real condition.
cards.back: Se piove, resteremo a casa.

cards.front: According to the notice …
cards.back: Secondo il comunicato …

cards.front: Does an attributed claim become proven?
cards.back: No. Attribution identifies the source, not truth.

cards.front: A practical negotiation request needs what?
cards.back: Problem, impact, concrete request and confirmation.

cards.front: Ask what a word means in this context.
cards.back: Che cosa significa qui questa parola?

cards.front: Is every informal expression a dialect form?
cards.back: No. Register, regional Italian and dialect are distinct.

cards.front: Neutral/polite farewell instead of ci becchiamo.
cards.back: Arrivederci. Context may also allow ci vediamo.

cards.front: A plan is preferred but not decided. Say that.
cards.back: Preferirei questa opzione, ma non ho ancora deciso.

cards.front: Two options: what should a recommendation include?
cards.back: Reasons, a constraint, an alternative and next action.

cards.front: Does attuale normally mean actual?
cards.back: Usually current. Actual often needs reale or effettivo.

cards.front: Four parts of a qualified argument.
cards.back: Claim, evidence/reason, warrant and limitation.

cards.front: Hypothetical: if I had time, I would study.
cards.back: Se avessi tempo, studierei.

cards.front: Unreal past: if I had had time, I would have studied.
cards.back: Se avessi avuto tempo, avrei studiato.

cards.front: Passive: Un addetto controlla i dati.
cards.back: I dati vengono controllati da un addetto.

cards.front: Plural passive-si: Si ___ i documenti.
cards.back: Si controllano i documenti.

cards.front: A receipt confirmation means approval?
cards.back: No. Distinguish receipt, review and approval.

cards.front: Quality was not measured. Can you claim quality improved?
cards.back: No. Preserve the unmeasured-outcome limitation.

cards.front: A small volunteer sample represents everyone?
cards.back: Not without justification. Mark scope and selection limits.

cards.front: Finalmente in a headline may suggest what?
cards.back: That a change was overdue; this is framing, not evidence.

cards.front: A remembered square and a trade register must conflict?
cards.back: No. They may capture different times/aspects/perspectives.

cards.front: Check your understanding politely.
cards.back: Se ho capito bene, …

cards.front: Staff ask who covers closing. Fair paraphrase?
cards.back: They need staffing arrangements clarified; not necessarily oppose access.

cards.front: A meeting note should separate what four things?
cards.back: Agreement, open issues, responsible actor and next date/status.

cards.front: Is passive always better formal writing?
cards.back: No. Name the actor when it helps action clarity.

cards.front: A pilot can show attendance but not necessarily what?
cards.back: Causal impact on learning or long-term effectiveness.

cards.front: One way to test genuine transfer after feedback.
cards.back: A new context/prompt without the model, then a delayed check.

cards.front: Interesting, but costs need clarification: rejection proved?
cards.back: No. A reservation is plausible; clarify required conditions.

cards.front: Compress a source while retaining what?
cards.back: Scope, source, key relationship, caveat and decision status.

cards.front: Review next week means opening next week?
cards.back: No. Review date is not a launch date.

cards.front: Willing to consider a trial means shifts accepted?
cards.back: No. Procedural interest differs from operational commitment.

cards.front: Past belief, earlier completion: Pensavo che ___ finito.
cards.back: Pensavo che avesse finito.

cards.front: Past viewpoint, simultaneous evaluation: Pensavo che ___ utile.
cards.back: Pensavo che fosse utile.

cards.front: Three registers, what must remain invariant?
cards.back: Facts, commitments, conditions, timing and uncertainty.

cards.front: Does formal prose prove greater truth?
cards.back: No. Judge evidence and scope separately from register.

cards.front: Regional speech proves lower education?
cards.back: No. That social inference is unsupported by a register choice.

cards.front: Answer a staffing objection with an access slogan?
cards.back: Insufficient. Address the actual staffing constraint.

cards.front: Three possible dimensions of disagreement.
cards.back: Means, goals and distribution of burdens.

cards.front: Approval subject to a roster. Say the condition.
cards.back: L'avvio è subordinato alla definizione dei turni.

cards.front: No owner assigned to evaluation. Invent one?
cards.back: No. Mark the responsibility unresolved and request assignment.

cards.front: How to avoid false consensus in minutes.
cards.back: State agreed points and explicitly identify remaining disagreement.

cards.front: More access is observed. Better learning established?
cards.back: No. A different outcome needs its own evidence.

cards.front: A principled revision shows weakness?
cards.back: No. Explain the evidence/reason for changing the position.

cards.front: Non tutti hanno approvato means nobody approved?
cards.back: No. It denies universal approval; other positions remain unspecified.

cards.front: Not excluded means proven?
cards.back: No. Possibility survives; proof has not been established.

cards.front: Source authority: minutes vs public summary.
cards.back: Compare their functions; a summary cannot silently expand a resolution.

cards.front: User says a date was promised; minutes have none.
cards.back: Evidence of an expectation, not proof of a documented promise.

cards.front: Two origins of ambiguous wording.
cards.back: Careless formulation or genuinely unresolved decision; investigate.

cards.front: Literary interpretation needs what besides imagination?
cards.back: Textual evidence, viewpoint awareness and alternative readings.

cards.front: An ironic reading is plausible. Intent certain?
cards.back: Not necessarily. Context/prosody and alternatives matter.

cards.front: An analogy for nonexperts must preserve what?
cards.back: The important relation and an explicit limit; not false certainty.

cards.front: Association alone identifies a causal effect?
cards.back: No. Consider alternatives and the comparison needed.

cards.front: Useful operational evidence can still lack what?
cards.back: Robust causal/generalising evidence. Usefulness and proof differ.

cards.front: Shorten a decision note without changing what?
cards.back: Agency, approval status, conditions, time and uncertainty.

cards.front: A negotiation must end in complete agreement?
cards.back: No. Define next steps while preserving principled disagreement.

cards.front: High attendance removes all access objections?
cards.back: No. Unserved groups and distributional values can remain relevant.

cards.front: What evidence would weaken your recommendation?
cards.back: State a concrete disconfirming observation, not only confirming evidence.

cards.front: Revision note: distinguish what two changes?
cards.back: Changed interpretation/commitment versus optional style.

cards.front: C2 means native identity and every dialect mastered?
cards.back: No. It concerns very high communicative competence, not identity or universality.

cards.front: Alphabet, vowels & the syllable model: recall the model or rule for “casa”.
cards.back: CA–sa — house/home
cards.note: A a; B bi; C ci; D di; E e; F effe; G gi; H acca; I i; L elle; M emme; N enne; O o; P pi; Q cu; R erre; S esse; T ti; U u; V vu (also vi); Z zeta. Extras: J i lunga, K cappa, W doppia vu, X ics, Y ipsilon (also i greca).

cards.front: Alphabet, vowels & the syllable model: recall the model or rule for “amica”.
cards.back: a–MI–ca — female friend
cards.note: A, e, i, o, u are vowel letters. Standard Italian distinguishes open/closed e and o in stressed syllables. Do not force English letter names or one fixed English vowel onto every Italian word.

cards.front: Alphabet, vowels & the syllable model: recall the model or rule for “Italia”.
cards.back: I–TA–lia — Italy
cards.note: 1. Look at the normal word. 2. Break it into the supplied syllable boxes. 3. Notice the stressed box. 4. Rejoin smoothly. Example: amica → a–MI–ca → amica. Capitals in a model mark stress, not normal spelling.

cards.front: Explain and repair: Italian i = English letter name eye
cards.back: Italian i is the vowel represented by /i/, with a heard Italian model.
cards.note: Separate letter names from word sounds, then build a word in syllables.

cards.front: Syllables: vowels, doubles & consonant groups: recall the model or rule for “palla”.
cards.back: PAL–la — ball
cards.note: Ca-sa, pa-ne, a-mi-ca. Build around the vowel centres, rather than reading isolated consonants.

cards.front: Syllables: vowels, doubles & consonant groups: recall the model or rule for “libro”.
cards.back: LI–bro — book
cards.note: Pal-la, pen-na, caf-fè. Keep the consonant long across the boundary; do not add a pause or an extra vowel. Cq also separates in conventional spelling division, as in ac-qua.

cards.front: Syllables: vowels, doubles & consonant groups: recall the model or rule for “paura”.
cards.back: pa–U–ra — fear
cards.note: Li-bro and scuo-la. Written ch, gh and palatal gn/gl/sc groups stay together in conventional division. Do not split chiave into c-hi-a-ve.

cards.front: Explain and repair: pa-l-la
cards.back: pal-la: two syllables, not three.
cards.note: Use checked syllable divisions instead of cutting a word after every letter.

cards.front: Word stress: the strong syllable: recall the model or rule for “gelato”.
cards.back: ge–LA–to — ice cream
cards.note: Our capitalised and outlined box marks the stressed syllable: ge-LA-to. Ordinary writing remains gelato.

cards.front: Word stress: the strong syllable: recall the model or rule for “telefono”.
cards.back: te–LE–fo–no — telephone
cards.note: Many Italian words stress the penultimate syllable, but TE-le-fo-no and u-ni-ver-si-TÀ show why a default is not a universal rule.

cards.front: Word stress: the strong syllable: recall the model or rule for “università”.
cards.back: u–ni–ver–si–TÀ — university
cards.note: Caffè and università retain their written accents. Most internal word stress is not written in normal text: telefono, not telèfono in an ordinary message. Dictionaries may add marks as pronunciation guidance.

cards.front: Explain and repair: Every Italian word stresses its second-last syllable
cards.back: Learn the supplied stress for each word.
cards.note: Notice the stressed syllable without changing the word’s normal spelling.

cards.front: Long consonants: pala is not palla: recall the model or rule for “pala”.
cards.back: PA–la — shovel: single l
cards.note: PA-la versus PAL-la: both have two syllables with first-syllable stress. The double spelling cues a longer consonant, not a third syllable.

cards.front: Long consonants: pala is not palla: recall the model or rule for “palla”.
cards.back: PAL–la — ball: long l
cards.note: For palla, maintain a longer l contact; for penna, a longer n. Stop consonants such as tt involve a longer closure, not two extra vowels.

cards.front: Long consonants: pala is not palla: recall the model or rule for “penna”.
cards.back: PEN–na — pen: long n
cards.note: Look at the checked boxes → notice the long consonant crossing the boundary → rejoin the word. Begin slowly, then return to a natural whole word. Avoid an artificial pause between every syllable.

cards.front: Explain and repair: palla has three syllables
cards.back: Pal-la has two; the length is in l.
cards.note: Separate syllable stress from consonant length and practise a safe slow-to-whole model.

cards.front: Gn & gli: bagno, figlio, famiglia: recall the model or rule for “bagno”.
cards.back: BA–gno — bathroom/bath
cards.note: BA-gno, RA-gno and GNOC-chi keep gn together in conventional written syllable division. Do not insert a separate g sound.

cards.front: Gn & gli: bagno, figlio, famiglia: recall the model or rule for “figlio”.
cards.back: FI–glio — son
cards.note: FI-glio, A-glio, fa-MI-glia. In glio/glia here the i is not an extra ee syllable. A speaker model is more reliable than the instruction “say English ly”.

cards.front: Gn & gli: bagno, figlio, famiglia: recall the model or rule for “famiglia”.
cards.back: fa–MI–glia — family
cards.note: Between vowels, these palatal consonants are normally long in standard Italian. The spelling fa-mi-glia keeps the written group together even though phonetic analyses can place a long consonant across a syllable boundary.

cards.front: Explain and repair: fa-mi-gli-a
cards.back: Fa-mi-glia has three syllables in the model.
cards.note: Keep palatal letter groups together in checked written syllable models.

cards.front: Sc, sch, c/ch & g/gh in syllables: recall the model or rule for “pesce”.
cards.back: PE–sce — fish: sc = /ʃ/ here
cards.note: C before e/i normally gives /tʃ/; g gives /dʒ/. Ch and gh before e/i keep /k/ and /g/. Compare caffè, gelato and chiave; gli spaghetti contains gh for /g/.

cards.front: Sc, sch, c/ch & g/gh in syllables: recall the model or rule for “scuola”.
cards.back: SCUO–la — school: sc = /sk/ here
cards.note: SCE-na and PE-sce use /ʃ/. In these common patterns, do not read s and c as separate /s/ + /k/. Between vowels the /ʃ/ is normally long in standard Italian.

cards.front: Sc, sch, c/ch & g/gh in syllables: recall the model or rule for “schiena”.
cards.back: SCHIE–na — back: sch keeps /sk/
cards.note: SCUO-la uses /sk/. SCHIE-na also keeps /sk/ before i. The following vowel sequence stays in one syllable in these word models.

cards.front: Explain and repair: pes-ce
cards.back: Pe-sce keeps the written palatal group together.
cards.note: Read common sound–spelling groups using complete syllables and checked words.

cards.front: From syllables to connected speech & IPA: recall the model or rule for “pane”.
cards.back: PA–ne → pane → il pane — from syllable scaffold to phrase
cards.note: Start with pa-ne, then pane as a whole word, then il pane. Keep a small meaningful group together, rather than placing equal pauses after every syllable.

cards.front: From syllables to connected speech & IPA: recall the model or rule for “caffè”.
cards.back: caf–FÈ → caffè → un caffè — keep final stress and double f
cards.note: Practise Sono qui | ho un libro as two sense groups. In ho un libro the vowel sequence crosses a word boundary; do not delete written letters or put in a compulsory stop between words. Actual linking depends on speech.

cards.front: From syllables to connected speech & IPA: recall the model or rule for “Sono qui. Ho un libro.”.
cards.back: Sono qui | ho un libro — two meaning groups; | is a practice marker, not normal punctuation
cards.note: Slashes / / enclose a broad phonemic representation. The mark ˈ indicates following primary stress; it is not an apostrophe in ordinary spelling. /i/ is a vowel, /j/ a glide; /ʃ/ as in scena, /ɲ/ as in bagno, /ʎ/ as in figlio; /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ are affricates.

cards.front: Explain and repair: Slash symbols and stress apostrophes belong in an ordinary email
cards.back: IPA belongs in pronunciation notes, not ordinary spelling.
cards.note: Rejoin words into short phrases and recognise a few pronunciation symbols.

cards.front: Punctuation: sentences, commas & quotations: recall the model or rule for “Ho pane, pasta e acqua.”.
cards.back: List comma — bread, pasta and water
cards.note: A statement can end with a full stop: Sono qui. A direct question uses ?: Lei è qui? Use ! selectively for an exclamation. Put a space after normal sentence punctuation, not before it.

cards.front: Punctuation: sentences, commas & quotations: recall the model or rule for “Sara, vieni qui!”.
cards.back: Direct address — Sara, come here!
cards.note: Ho pane, pasta e acqua. Sara, vieni qui! Commas separate these list items and set off a person being addressed. Do not insert one between subject and verb: Sara studia.

cards.front: Punctuation: sentences, commas & quotations: recall the model or rule for “Sara dice: «Ciao!»”.
cards.back: Colon + paired quotation marks — Sara says “Hi!”
cards.note: A colon can introduce direct speech: Sara dice: «Ciao!» Italian quotation styles can use «…» or “…” depending on house style. Keep opening/closing marks paired; this course supplies the exact style for each exercise.

cards.front: Explain and repair: Sara, studia. (Sara is the subject)
cards.back: Sara studia. No comma between this subject and verb.
cards.note: Use sentence marks and simple commas without breaking the sentence’s grammar.

cards.front: Writing basics: capitals, accents & apostrophes: recall the model or rule for “È qui.”.
cards.back: È = is — a written accent changes the word
cards.note: Caffè, università and perché keep their final accents. È is the verb is; e means and. Sì means yes; si has other grammatical uses. Standard spellings here use è/caffè with grave è and perché with acute é.

cards.front: Writing basics: capitals, accents & apostrophes: recall the model or rule for “un’amica / un amico”.
cards.back: Feminine elision / masculine un — apostrophe depends on the construction
cards.note: Un’amica, l’amico and c’è show elision. Un amico has no apostrophe. Un po’ is the conventional shortening of poco: write the apostrophe, not pò. Standard edited Italian uses qual è without an apostrophe.

cards.front: Writing basics: capitals, accents & apostrophes: recall the model or rule for “Studio italiano lunedì.”.
cards.back: Lowercase language and weekday — sentence-start capitals are a separate rule
cards.note: Capitalise sentence beginnings and personal/place names: Ciao, Sara. Sono a Roma. Italian normally writes language names, weekdays and months lowercase: italiano, lunedì, ottobre. Contexts such as headings and names can differ.

cards.front: Explain and repair: un pò
cards.back: un po’ uses an apostrophe, not a grave accent.
cards.note: Distinguish stress accents, apostrophes and capitalisation in short messages.
